speechtext: I have the honour to inform the house that the Clerk of the House has received from the chief electoral officer a certificate of the election and return of Thomas Clement Douglas, Esquire, for the electoral district of Burnaby-Coquitlam.
Mr. Thomas Clement Douglas, member for the electoral district of Burnaby-Coquitlam, introduced by Mr. Stanley Knowles and Mr. H. W. Herridge.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with the leave of the house I should like to take this opportunity of extending a welcome to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). When I came into the House of Commons 22 years ago he had then been a member of this house for a period of five years. Since then he has occupied the high position of premier of the province of Saskatchewan. Indeed, the length of his service there in that capacity gave those of us of other political parties some idea of
the meaning of eternity. I welcome him to the house and assure him that in the days ahead we shall look forward to the contribution he will make.
The House of Commons has little changed in the past few years. From generation to generation it remains much the same, subject to those changes that inevitably must take place. But in one particular it remains the same; the spirit of good fellowship prevails at all times irrespective of the differences that separate us. The hon. gentleman, for many years in my province and now in another province, comes to the House of Commons knowing he is returning to a place where the spirit of democracy prevails. I welcome him.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to be able to agree with the Prime Minister-
Oh, oh.

-especially in a matter so controversial in more ways than one, as the return to the house of the leader of the New Democratic party. We on this side of the house welcome him and we are sure, Mr. Speaker, that our debates will be more lively and stimulating because of his presence.

Mr. Speaker, it is a real privilege to welcome the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam to our midst. I am sure he has a very definite, positive contribution to make here in this house. As I look back over the years I realize that he will find many changes since he was here last. In fact many things have taken place since 1936, that year which now seems so long ago. At that time I too was an aspirant to this house, although perhaps not so successful as was the hon. member.
It is amusing to recall the fact, as I remember it recorded in the papers, that at one time he carried a dual candidature into the federal election. In fact, on one side of the car there was a Social Credit banner and on the other side of the car there was a C.C.F. banner. I am not quite as old as the hon. member, but being interested in these things I remember the conversation that took place around the breakfast table at home. My dad had commented on this and my mother, rather in horror, said, "I think that gentleman must be two-faced". My younger

Introduction of Member brother spoke up and said, "My, I would like to be like that gentleman because it would be fun to travel on a train; you could see out of both sides at the same time."
In the changes that have taken place he will find in his own group, as I have been very interested to find in the past few weeks, that many of the members he is now privileged to lead have gone a long way afield from the Regina manifesto, which might have had something to do with taking the hon. member away from his place in that hallowed hall in Saskatchewan. But he will get used to that. I think probably his experience will help him in solving some of these problems.
He will also find changes on the government side. He has not had to put up with very many members from that noble party in the Saskatchewan legislature. I think, however, if he had done a better job in that province there might not have been so many of them here as there are now. Then with the Liberals too he will find a great deal of change. Out in Saskatchewan the members of this noble party tried to kick down the doors of the legislature to get in. Here in Ottawa, in our national parliament, they try to kick down the doors and blow off the roof to get out. Such are the changes which take place, Mr. Speaker.
I was very disturbed last week when I read in the press that it was on Monday, November 5, that the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam would be introduced in the house. I was very relieved the other night, I think in the wee hours in the morning, when the hon. member who served as house leader of the party across the way mentioned to me that he thought it would be today rather than then. I am grateful to the chief electoral officer that this is possible, because on November 5, which is next Monday, we will be celebrating the 357th anniversary of a certain gentleman by the name of Guy Fawkes who attempted very hard to blow the roof off another parliament.
Mr. Speaker, we welcome the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I am sure, as has already been expressed by the Prime Minister and the leader of the official opposition that the full and cordial welcome which is customary in this house will be extended to him by all of us.

After he had been here a year he stood up in the house one evening and said: "Mr. Speaker, after having sat in this chamber for one year I am convinced that the only person who ever approached parliament in the proper frame of mind was Guy Fawkes". I am very glad that I am not entering the house on Guy Fawkes day.
Mr. Speaker, it is just 27 years ago that I was first elected to this chamber. It is 18 years since I left it. I would think that any person who started as a private and wound up as a private could at least say that he was holding his own. As the Prime Minister said, many things do not change. Certainly the unfailing courtesy of this house has not changed. A great many things have not changed, including the accommodation for M.P.'s. I want to say that the good will and the marvellous esprit de corps of this house has not changed. I am very happy to be back in it. I want to thank all members for the warmth of their welcome.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: EXTENSION OF FORGIVENESS PERIOD RESPECTING LOANS FOR SEWAGE TREATMENT PROJECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement on the question of extension of the cut-off date for forgiveness of a portion of federal loans to municipalities under the National Housing Act for the purpose of construction of sewage treatment projects.
Hon. members will recall that the National Housing Act was amended in December, 1960 to enable Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to make long term low interest loans to assist municipalities in financing the cost of these projects. The loan is up to two thirds of the cost and, as a special incentive, the government was authorized to forgive payment of 25 per cent of the amount of

Statement on National Housing Act the loan committed and 25 per cent ol the interest paid or accrued due thereon in respect of all work completed up to March 31, 1963.
The purpose of the legislation was to launch a program constituting a first real co-ordinated attack on the three problems of conservation of water, prevention of pollution, and assistance to municipalities in providing services essential to the maintenance and expansion of municipal growth. The purpose of the forgiveness provision with a deadline of next March was to serve the dual ends of providing an incentive to make an early start on these problems and thus of providing additional employment at a time when it was and still is a national objective.
The success of the program can be judged by the fact that between December, 1960 and October 19, 1962 some 335 loans have been approved to 273 municipalities, in which one third of the population of Canada lives. The amount of these loans has aggregated $79.5 million, and it is estimated that the earned forgiveness by March 31, 1963 will be $15 million for two full years of operation. In addition, 16 formal applications for loans totalling nearly $2.4 million are on hand and inquiries relating to 202 other projects, with a loan potential of $55.7 million, have been received.
It so happens, however, that the bulk of loans so far applied for and approved has been made to municipalities in only three provinces. In the main this appears to be because those provinces had systems under which they were able to encourage and assist their municipalities to take advantage of the assistance offered. Some other provinces are now so organizing. We have accordingly been receiving very pressing representations from municipalities, from some provincial governments and from members of parliament to extend the cut-off date so as to avoid hardship and discrimination against those areas where municipalities, in spite of a sincere effort, would not be able to complete work now in hand, or have not found it possible to complete plans and specifications and call tenders, in time for the March 31 date for discontinuance of the rebate.
The government is fully conscious of the program offers to municipalities in meeting their development problems. We have therefore decided to ask parliament at this session to extend the expiry "date for partial debt their development problems. We have therefore decided to ask parliament at this session to extend the expiry date for partial debt cancellation on this type of loan to March 31, 1965-an additional two year yeriod.


It should be emphasized that with or without the forgiveness feature this is a continuing program of municipal assistance. The proposed extension of the forgiveness period should, however, provide an additional incentive to take an early part in this important anti-pollution measure, with consequent further advantages with respect to employment, while at the same time enabling municipalities to plan their programs in the most effective manner.
I would also ask the co-operation of hon. members on all sides of the house in bringing this proposed extension to the attention of the municipal authorities in their areas, so there may be the widest possible participation in what is proving to be a most effective antipollution measure and an urgent contribution to the health and well-being of all Canadians.

Certainly everything possible should be done to assist the municipalities in the very difficult problems they face. I trust this is just a forerunner of more measures directed along the same line. Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate this group with the remarks that have been made in commending the minister for extending the date within which this program for antipollution measures may be undertaken. The other day I had occasion to read a very detailed report, prepared by the government of the United States, which shows that the rivers of that great country have virtually become sewers, not only because of the sewage discharged from large cities but also because of the drainage from agricultural

areas where tremendous quantities of insecticides and weed killing chemicals have been used.
This whole question of river pollution is one which the country will have to face up to, and it is certainly something which neither the municipalities nor the provinces can adequately handle on their own. The steps which are being taken by the minister will be a move in that direction, although it seems to me a much larger program and much greater planning of the program will have to be undertaken to meet it effectively.
I also think that when we come to speak of assistance to municipalities we shall have to think in terms of a broad program that will include a number of things, rather than a piecemeal program, but this is something we can discuss on some other occasion. I simply rise to associate this group with the remarks made and say that we are in complete agreement with the proposal made by the minister and wish to commend him for it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement to the house concerning the quarantine measures being applied by the United States against shipments of offensive weapons and war material to Cuba.
The United States navy has been directed to stop and search and, if necessary, divert ships of any nationality entering the quarantine area around Cuba. The United States government has now instituted arrangements whereby, as a service to international shipping and in order to avoid delays due to stoppage and search at sea, advance clearance may be obtained at the last port of call before entering the quarantine area. Application for a clearance certificate may be made by a ship's agent, or other ship's officer, to a local United States consular officer who is empowered to issue a clearance certificate after inspection of the ship and its cargo. These procedures are available to ships of any flag, including those of the Soviet bloc.
The Canadian government has agreed to these advance clearance facilities being made available to ships in Canadian ports for as long as the quarantine arrangements are in force. There is, of course, no question of compulsory inspection of any ships when in Canadian waters, but rather of their being free to take advantage of these facilities in order to avoid possible subsequent delay and inconvenience.

APPOINTMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION ON PILOTAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement regarding the appointment of a commission to inquire into matters relating to marine pilotage. Hon. members will recall that last spring certain difficulties arose between ship operators and pilots on the St. Lawrence river. In the course of the discussions with both parties which led to the resolution of those difficulties, I informed the house that it was the intention of the government to appoint a royal commission to look into matters of marine pilotage generally.
It had, in fact, been apparent for some time that, on the one hand, the various marine pilotage groups across Canada and, on the other hand, the ship owners and operators felt that a general review by an independent inquiry of all matters relating to marine pilotage would be desirable. The rapidly changing technological, social and economic conditions of the twentieth century had raised many new problems in this regard which could not be foreseen when earlier legislation regarding pilotage matters had been developed and brought into force many years ago. The appointment of the commission was, in fact, desired last spring by both the ship owners and the pilots connected with the difficulties which occurred then, and the desirability of this course of action was specifically confirmed to me in my contacts with pilots and shipping interests generally.
The members of the commission will be as follows: chairman, Hon. Yves Bernier, judge of the Quebec superior court, of Lau-zon, province of Quebec; members, Mr. H. A. Renwick, vice president and general manager of British Columbia Manufacturing Company Limited, of Vancouver, B.C., and Mr. R. K. Smith, former chairman of the national harbours board, of Waterloo, Ontario, and Parrsboro, Nova Scotia. Its terms of reference will be sufficiently broad to allow it to deal with all relevant matters relating to marine pilotage in Canada, but rather than take the time of the house by reading them in full, if the house agrees I will now table the order in council appointing the commission.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could begin by asking that the order in council be printed in Hansard, if possible. As the minister is aware, I am one member who is concerned with the great many pilots in Port Weller, Sault Ste. Marie and my own area. This would be the simplest way of enabling hon. members to study the

terms of reference, which are going to be of a great deal of interest both in connection with shipping and more directly with pilotage.
One of the other points I should like to make is this. While we welcome this move I should like to argue-though this is not the time to argue-that one of the most important problems relating to pilotage is our relationship with our neighbour across the lakes, the United States. Since I cannot argue, I can at least hope that there will be opportunities for United States witnesses to make representations and appear before the commission, because the problem is that we are moving toward a pilotage based upon servants of the crown, and they have a pilotage based upon trade union organization. When there is an interlocking of responsibility, as does exist on the great lakes, there is a great possibility of conflict and confusion, and even labour tie-ups.
We welcome this commission and would hope that, unlike many of the other commissions we have had, its hearings will go quickly and we will have a report before next spring. I say this because I think we are all aware that there is a great deal of discontent amongst pilots, not only in the St. Lawrence river area but in the Port Weller-Sarnia area, and this same discontent has spread into the upper lakes and is rife amongst the United States pilots and their organizations who share the duties with Canadian pilots on the lakes.

Mr. Chairman, when at
five o'clock last Wednesday I sat down, after having spoken only for a few minutes, I had come to the chapter of commendations.

May I now congratulate Mr. Clement Brown, the defeated candidate in the riding of Dollard, for his promotion in the press gallery when he changed over from Le Devoir to Montreal Matin. I wish him the best of luck, and I hope that he will be as fair-minded in the Montreal Matin as he was in Le Devoir. I am sorry not to be a steady reader of Montreal Matin, because I will not have the pleasure of reading his articles as I did before. But, anyway, I wish him the best success.
During the last election, Mr. Brown repeated on several occasions, on the radio and on television, that, for several years, he had attended the house as an observer, and as such, he had chosen the Conservative party.
I always found it difficult to understand such a choice, because the record of the Conservative party is in no way to be envied.
During this debate we have heard many speakers from all sides of the house and, more particularly, we have heard government members commending the government and expressing their pride in its achievements.
We have heard the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Sevigny), with superb oratory, extoll the merits of the government of which he is a member and, to prove his statements, he quoted from an article which was published in the American magazine Time on October 26 last. As my fellow member for Essex West (Mr. Gray) pointed out, the Associate Minister of National Defence, as seems to be the practice among government members, quoted only part of that article which can be found on page 15, while omitting as can be seen, the part in which the Diefenbaker administration was con-denmned.
The hon. member for Essex West quoted the rest of that article and, for everybody's information, I shall read again that passage of the article:
What Diefenbaker did not go out of his way to mention was that some key indicators are unhappily slowing up. The index of industrial production rose steeply to 186.6 in May, from 169.2 a year earlier, but slowed to a crawl by midsummer. Unemployment, while lower than it has been, was still, at 3.9 per cent of the labour force, not low enough. A 4 per cent rise in public spending during the first six months, mostly on a crash program to build vocational schools, was flattened by Ottawa's $228 million austerity cut-back-and that, said a Montreal economist, is $228 million worth of jobs.

In short, the Canadian people will be deprived this year of $228 million, because this amount was lopped off the estimates.
Therefore, many employees of private enterprise will lose their jobs as a result of the government's maladministration. Many industries have already been forced to close their doors and lay off a great number of employees. In support of my statement, may I, Mr. Chairman, tell the house about the difficulties confronting Canadair. At the beginning of the year, it was compelled to dismiss 2,400 workers and it will be forced, before the end of the year, to dismiss about another 1,200, thus increasing by 3,600 the number of jobless in Canada. These 3,600 workers in the metropolitan area thus will be deprived of their salary and such dismissal will deprive also the merchants and the industrialists of an amount of $265,000, representing the salaries those employees would have received.
Mr. Chairman, I am convinced that if this government had wanted to take a specific and constructive measure in that respect, it could have asked the directors of T.C.A. to purchase planes manufactured by Canadair and paid for with the Canadian taxpayers' money, instead of buying them in the United States or in England. It could also have compelled the R.C.A.F. authorities to purchase airplanes made by that important Canadian aircraft company instead of British or American made aircraft. That is another example of the negligence of the Conservative government we have in power in Canada.
Since the return to power of the Conservatives, in 1957, our country has had unprecedented unemployment and our economy has slowed down considerably. A few days after the last general election, the government which no longer had the confidence of the public and which was in a minority position in the house, had to admit to the Canadian people that our finances were not as good as they were led to believe during the electoral campaign and that, because of its fiscal and monetary policy, the government had to impose an austerity program without delay.
Mr. Chairman, that situation has been directly brought about by a lack of administrative efficiency on the part of the members of the cabinet, by their inconceivable carelessness in managing the business of the nation, by a lack of cohesion among themselves, by the want of confidence which they have brought upon themselves on the part of high officials of the civil service and, as a result also, by a constant hesitancy on the
Ways and Means
part of Canadian and foreign businessmen who have never been able to know where they were going.
To cope with this economical decline, the government should have taken drastic steps and established a specific program, on a short term as well as on a long term basis. It has not done so. There is nothing surprising in the fact that the Canadian people have shown their discontent by voting, in the proportion of 63 per cent, against the Conservative government.
But, on account of certain factors, the government has not been completely overthrown, as the population was hoping it would, and we now have a minority government, supported by those new Conservatives, the Social Crediters. Our greatest surprise, in the beginning of the session, and ever since, came from the union of the Conservative party with the followers and white caps of Mrs. Gilberte Cote-Mercier and of Mr. Louis Even, who have schooled the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette), blindly followed by the other Social Credit members from the province of Quebec.
Mr. Chairman, the Social Credit members from Quebec are Social Crediters in the province of Quebec. They put forward a Social Credit doctrine in the house, but they vote in favour of the Conservative party each time they can do so. To my way of thinking, that attitude results in the greatest political concubinage ever seen in Canada since confederation.
When they came forward as candidates in the province of Quebec, they took a formal commitment to fight the government. They condemned the policy of the Conservative party. After the campaign, after the election of a certain number of Social Crediters, the hon. member for Villeneuve, leader of the group, at a press conference on the French network of the C.B.C., committed himself to overthrow the government at the first opportunity. To support what I am saying, I should like to quote from page 76 of a book entitled "Real Caouette vous parle". In answer to a question from Mr. Gerard Morin, parliamentary correspondent for Le Droit, who asked him if the Social Crediters would put forward a non-confidence motion, the hon. member for Villeneuve stated:
Perhaps not, but if somebody comes forward with a non-confidence motion, you can rest assured that I will vote against the government, whether it is headed by Diefenbaker or Pearson. There is no possible coalition between the Social Crediters and any federal political party.
And there has not been any.

Mr. Caouette goes on to say:
It is with our principles and for our principles that we are elected, and we will maintain our stand.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid that the era of principles is over, and while the Social Credit members keep on expounding their strange theory in the house, they wilfully and constantly maintain in power a government which they had themselves asked the people to condemn, fight and topple down.
In the last election campaign, they had promised to fight unemployment which, according to them, was a Conservative evil. But today, in the house, they maintain in power a Conservative government which is responsible for the most serious unemployment situation we have ever known in this country, and for their part, the Conservatives are happy. They show it by their smile, their embraces and their delicate attention towards the Social Crediters. They are happy to be maintained in power by these spiritual sons of Mrs. Gilberte Cote-Mercier and of Mr. Louis Even.
The Social Crediters had promised the people to fight against credit restrictions.

The only thing left for the Conservatives to do would be to wear the white beret of the union of electors.

Australia protects her domestic sugar industry by controlling prices and prohibiting imports. Austria, West Germany, France and the Netherlands protect their domestic sugar industries by a tariff, a flexible duty sufficient to equalize the costs of domestic and imported sugar, and they also use import controls. The duty amounts to the difference between the domestic supported price and the cost of imported sugar. Denmark protects her domestic industry with a small tariff and an import monopoly. The Irish protect their sugar beet industry by consumer price control, and import licences are issued only to the Irish Sugar Company. The Mexican sugar industry is protected by a 50 per cent ad valorem duty and a fixed valuation for duty purposes of $10 per 100 pounds. Consumer price control is also in effect.
In summing up, it is admitted that the sugar beet industry cannot compete with raw cane as a source of sugar supply. It just is not possible for a great many reasons. That fact is accepted by all concerned; and practically all countries which are situated in the northern temperate zone, countries which are industrialized and where living standards are fairly high, for the purposes of national defence as well as to guarantee at all times a diversified source of sugar supply have made arrangements to protect their own sugar beet industries.
The sugar beet producers of Canada say that the time has now come when the government must decide whether the sugar beet industry in Canada is worth saving. If it is worth saving, then additional support will have to be provided. A great deal of support has been provided in recent years. The government has studied the situation carefully and since 1958, I believe, subsidies have been paid to the sugar beet industry. The method of paying subsidies has been varied several times in an effort to find a formula which will best serve the purpose. No formula so far has completely satisfied the requirements.
The method being used for 1962 is too new to be fully appraised. The present method may be satisfactory, but it is felt by the sugar beet producers that, as they have recommended, the support price should be raised from 4| cents to 5J cents per pound. I recommend wholeheartedly to the members of this committee, to the house and to the government that the fullest consideration be given to the sugar beet industry in Canada. A

decision is urgent as to whether this industry is worth saving. If it is worth saving, then means will have to be found to provide adequate encouragement for producers of sugar beet to continue their operation.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the hon. member a question just to keep the record straight? Did I understand the hon. member to say that the price paid to beet growers was about $11, and is that true of Alberta and Manitoba as well as Ontario?

No, Mr. Chairman. The
method of supporting sugar beet production, as I said, has been changed several times to try to find a formula which would satisfy the requirements of every area. This has been found most difficult. Until last year the workings of the support price system were found to be much more satisfactory in Alberta and Manitoba than they were in Ontario. Ontario had a terrific growth of beets in 1961; the average crop was over 17 tons per acre, which is very high. However, due to the climatic conditions prevailing in 1961 the sugar content was exceedingly low.
Therefore the formula and the method of subsidy used did not fulfil the requirements of the Canadian industry. Let me repeat; the method of subsidization has been changed on several occasions in an effort to find one which would cover the conditions prevailing in each of the four sugar beet areas. Quebec is best off at the present time. Quebec sugar beet processing is done by a crown corporation and they pay the growers, I understand, $13 a ton regardless of sugar content. In addition, the growers of Quebec receive from the federal government any subsidy which is given to producers in Ontario.
The sugar beet growers have met the government every year, and sometimes several times a year. This year there is complete unanimity among the Canadian sugar beet growers association along the lines I have stated, that this industry cannot continue without additional support.

The spokesman for the government

drew us a picture of that beautiful vision, and of that beautiful dream, in which he and his colleagues have believed since their accession to office.
I think, like many other members, that it is high time the members of the ministry cease deluding themselves and recognize at last the situation with which our population is faced.
It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that in the light of the results of the election of June 18 last, and the implementation of the austerity program from June 24 on, the minister is a bit daring when he claims that the economic situation has improved in Canada as much as he would want us to believe.
I admit that the minister is absolutely free to build up the administration he belongs to, but I doubt that he had any success in convincing several hon. members of this house of all the attributes of the government.
The revised estimates he submitted to us are in every way in accordance with the doctrine formerly adhered to by the Liberal party, a doctrine the Conservative party seems ready to adopt. Such a doctrine would have been justified in the fifteenth century, but it is not adapted to our own era. In my opinion, the philosophy of both parties is 100 per cent identical in the sense that it does not take into account the facts pertaining to this century and all those who adhere to this philosoply tend to reduce the purchasing power of the consumer to the level of production.
Mr. Chairman, the government's fiscal policy aims to cut down the estimates of the various departments responsible for public works in Canada. The government's policy in this respect will bring about a further cut in the number of jobs available to Canadians. Like several other members, I believe that the administration is wrong, and that it should, instead, favour and undertake, as soon as possible, large scale public works, as could easily be done throughout the country.
The Saguenay district, of which I am a representative, provides presently, as in the past, a good source of income for the government, as compared to the population. In view of the natural resources in our district which are exploited by large corporations, I am entitled to claim, on behalf of my fellow citizens, that the government invest sizeable amounts in public works, since those amounts come
Ways and Means
from taxes levied against corporations which live off the resources of our district.
The city of Alma, where I live, has spent a lot of money to build a very modern municipal air terminus, and all there is left to do now is to pave the runway. That airport could easily become the centre of all commercial activities in the northern part of the province. The military airport in Bagot-ville, which will be increasingly called upon for the national defence of the country, does not meet any more the requirements of commercial and civil aviation. The tragedy which happened there recently is one of the most striking proofs to support that view. The Alma airport is some 60 miles west from Bagotville, right in the heart of the kingdom of the Saguenay. It could very well become the port of call of commercial as well as of T.C.A. airplanes on their way to the north. That would be an excellent development for our area. It would enable all surplus farm production to be shipped to the north shore, an area which is bound to expand more and more, thus requiring an ever increasing quantity of farm commodities.
Our area also has retaining walls to protect from erosion a large portion of farm lands; but every j'ear, those retaining walls crumble into the magnificent lake St. John. Those walls had been built by the Liberal government but, alas, during the five years the Conservative party has been in power, it has not found it advisable to add a single stone to them.
I could also insist upon a great many other improvements by the government; but let me tell you only that the Saguenay area-as you may have read in the Labour Gazette-is considered as having a manpower surplus. I also would like to point out to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) that, according to the Labour Gazette, the Saguenay area and the town of Oshawa where he lives are considered as the two regions where labour is affected the most. Surely, this is not to the credit of the Minister of Labour.
Defeat them.

We ask the
government to consider at once those problems facing the areas thus defined.
Mr. Chairman, the constituency of Lake St. John, which I have the honour to represent in this house, is composed in equal parts of farmers and city dwellers.

Ways and Means
Agriculture would be fairly good, but unstable low prices, and the difficulty of marketing farm products, added to a constant increase in production costs, render the farmer's position rather difficult, not to say impossible.
The farmers of my area, who are hard working and active, and who appreciate the need to unite and to group themselves to protect their interests, have set up in my constituency, on a co-operative basis, a somewhat important complex of animal slaughtering and pork butchery which in the last few years, has had an increasing turnover. Last year, if I am not mistaken, that organization made more than $10 million. I think it is a fine achievement on the part of the farmers of our area, and I am sure that with the help of the government they will be able to keep on improving their situation.
I consider that the main problem at present facing the farmers of my area is that of feed grain. In our district, it is possible to obtain feed grain by water transportation. But I believe the government will have to help those organizations facilitate transportation of grain by water up to the harbours of the Saguenay area, that is Bagotville or Chicoutimi.
I am sure that, at present, this co-operative organization is headed by people who are conscious of that problem. In fact, they even have at their disposal, at present, an expert in the matter, who has had the opportunity of travelling in the various western provinces to study on the spot the possibility of buying on behalf of farmers of my area, what they need in the way of feed grain.
I think that I should point out here that the Saguenay area consumed, last year, over 70 million pounds of feed grain, which were shipped to us by rail.
I am sure that those people will soon approach the officials of the Department of Agriculture, to suggest something now under study, which is to set up locally in our area a complete storage system in the deep-water harbours of Bagotville and Chicoutimi, as well as a flour mill to answer grain and feed needs in the Saguenay district, which will result in doubling the consumption of grain in our area in the near future.
I wonder, Mr. Chairman, if you would call it one o'clock?

As it is now past one o'clock, I shall leave the chair.

(Text):

Before you leave the chair, Mr. Charman, I wonder whether I may be permitted to put a brief question to the Acting Minister of Finance. Is it the intention of the government today to make the returns to orders Nos. 29, 30 and 31 in the name of Mr. Turner? If so, could they be made as quickly as possible?

I shall have to make inquiry. I will inform my hon. friend later in the day.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, when the committee adjourned at dinner time, I was dealing with the farm problem in my constituency and, before changing the subject, I should like to finish what I have to say on the matter.
The government has always tried to increase our markets for farm products, and more particularly for feed grain. And every discussion we had in this house on that subject dealt with this aspect.
I should like to point out to the Minister of Agriculture, and also to the government, that they would stand to gain by turning to the east. If some research was done and some expenditure made to increase consumption of feed grain in the east, it would become apparent that that district-and more particularly the Saguenay area-presents a considerable potential for consumption, which might be doubled by an improved organization.
I submit that point of view to the department responsible for these matters, as it has, indeed, often been brought to its attention in this house.
Before tackling another theme, I want to congratulate the government for having at last appointed a French Canadian parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Agriculture, in the person of the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Pigeon). The appointment of the hon. member is a wise choice, because I am sure that he is well prepared to fill this position. We, and more particularly the representatives of the province of Quebec, were glad to hear it.

On the other hand, I would like to add that, as the government, at a given moment, chose to name an Associate Minister of National Defence while Canadians had not asked for it, then I think it should grant the wishes of the Canadian people by appointing an associate minister of agriculture who would alternately represent the great areas of this country, the east and the west.
Thus we would have the assurance that the eastern as well as the western farmers would be fairly treated by the department and the government, in all relevant fields.
Mr. Chairman, the federal government is more and more called upon to look after education. The problem of education is under provincial jurisdiction according to the confederation pact, and, on that account, the federal government should not be too much involved in that field.
It is clear that, if the Canadian people are turning more and more towards Ottawa to find a solution to the financial problems of education, it is mostly due to the fact that provincial governments are not sufficiently able to pay the ever increasing amount which Canada's development requires, more particularly in that field.
If the federal government has enough money to subsidize education at the provincial level, this is due to the fact that it keeps too great a share of taxes, thus making it impossible for the provinces to perform effectively the duties devolved to them by confederation.
Mr. Chairman, I trust that the government will consider that it is urgent to give back to the provinces their sources of revenue so as to enable them to carry out their responsibilities in all respects.
I know that the government has increased and intends to increase even more the deductions on personal income tax, for provincial income tax purposes, and I trust that in the next budget-if one is introduced-it will pursue the policy which consists in restoring part of the rights and privileges which the previous administration had taken away on the occasion of the last war and which it neglected to return, through a minor oversight, once the war was over. I know that a commission has been established to consider the problem of our taxation system.
However, like many others, I deplore the fact that the provinces were not invited to appoint their own representatives on that commission, which will have to suggest solutions big with consequences for their development. If I can rely on the figures that I succeeded
Ways and Means
in obtaining from various sources, the federal government collects yearly in Quebec some $2 billion through various taxes, but it gives back only $500 million. If those figures are correct, I suggest that we do not have to look any further for the cause of the financial problems of the various provincial, municipal and school authorities. The provinces will have to be given back as soon as possible their taxation fields, and I invite the present government to act along those lines, because I feel certain that it will then meet with the approval of all people in Canada.
At this stage of my remarks, I should like to quote an extract from a statement made by the premier of our province, last Friday, in Hull:
On the other hand, I would ask those who are governing on the other side of the river, I would ask my federal Liberal friends-
That is for you, gentlemen.
-who are on the other side of the river to realize it is time-
He was asking you to realize it is time.
-for the federal government to understand that provincial priority needs, in the field of taxation require that those rights be handed back to the provinces.
Now, listen to this:
During the war, priority needs-
You suffered no losses for 20 years.

-to defend democracy may have required that taxation rights be handed over to the central power. Today, if our democracy is to survive, if the economic expansion of provinces and municipalities is to be achieved, Ottawa must hand back to the provinces those rights which had been lent to the central government.
Our Liberal friends on my right-
They stole them.

-like to applaud to the words of the Quebec premier which is one of their good friends and we, from this part of the house, would fully agree with Mr. Lesage's words, if only he would today keep his word.
It seems that at the time when he was part of the Quebec representation here, and that he was a minister, his opinions were-I would not say diametrically opposed, but they were not similar to those expressed in the statement I have just quoted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
He was a centralist.

Ways and Means
But, however, I would not like to minimize what he said last Friday in Hull, because I think and hope he was sincere.

That does not happen often.
Another hon. Member: Oh, that is not certain.
There is nothing certain.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of the latitude granted to us in relation to the discussion on the budget to raise a matter which is controversial at the moment, and I mean the federal civil servants.
It is inconceivable that, in 1962, more than 50,000 civil servants should still be at the mercy of the government and of the dictatorial decisions of government members, while everywhere else in the country, employees of private enterprise have been granted the legal right to unite and make representations about their working conditions, salaries and promotions. Now, such a right is being denied the servants of the crown.
Mr. Chairman, I think the time has come to render justice to that group of workers, so that they may be treated like any other group of Canadians.
The recent Glassco report emphasized many deficiencies in administration which resulted in a waste of public funds, but I do not believe we should refuse to increase the civil servants' salaries in order to remedy that situation. In my opinion, to do so when the rate increase had been agreed upon in principle would be likely to aggravate the situation. I also do not find it normal that an organization which employs so many people should not have established long ago its own personnel training school as every important enterprise in this country has done.
I should not like to leave the subject of the public service without saying a few words on the bilingual character of our country. There is no need to repeat here all the legitimate grievances we have heard concerning the way French is treated in the administration generally. One has but to read the Glassco report to find a few concrete examples. What strikes me in all this is to hear Her Majesty the Queen and her husband Prince Philip, as well as Sir Harold Macmillan, Prime Minister of Great Britain, representing what I believe is a non-bilingual country, speaking perfect French, right in front of our leaders who do not even understand that language and that, in an officially bilingual country. It is a shame, at a time when in every country of the world, people endeavour to speak two

languages, to see that in Canada, only Quebec citizens have to be bilingual in order to succeed in the administration of our nation. It is high time that bilingualism should cease being theoretical and become a real fact in the interests of Canada.
As an actual recommendation, Mr. Chairman, we suggest the grant of a bonus to any bilingual employee for his better services to the nation. We hope that will urge everybody to become bilingual. I think that suggestion deserves consideration.
Mr. Chairman, since we started discussing new legislation, two projects were introduced. The purpose of both is to extend credit in order to assist production and marketing. Within the framework of today's economic concepts, it is obvious that those measures were necessary, and I would even say that they do not go far enough because they will not enable our industries to sell all the production surpluses that cripple them.
At this time the government should extend credit to all friendly countries, especially those in Latin America, to enable them to obtain in our country what they need to increase the standard of living of their people. That would undoubtedly be the best weapon ever used by a country to fight the rise of subversive ideas in our hemisphere.
While the people of Canada would be busy producing to meet orders for various goods that would follow the implementation of such a policy, the problems of unemployment and economic instability would solve themselves to the greatest advantage of all.
I know that many in this house will say that those countries have not the means to pay for all the goods we would put at their disposal. In my opinion, it would be the very way by which we could greatly improve the present state of our economy. I know that those countries have not the means to pay, but at present in Canada, we have a certain number of workers without jobs. We could use that policy to put people to work, to produce some consumer goods and export them into friendly countries. We would contribute to improve the situation.
If we have accepted during the last wars to work unstintingly in order to provide for all the necessary materials of war, I believe that we would accept to work in order to provide those friendly countries with anything they need, and even if we were doing it without compensation we would have, at least, the satisfaction to know that we had contributed to the building of those countries,

that we had assisted people in need instead of killing and demolishing as we did during the last world war.
To conclude, since my time is practically over-
May I ask you a question?

When I am through with my speech; my time is running out.
To conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the government that a country may declare a state of emergency or set itself up on a war footing when it is threatened or attacked by an enemy. That is normal and we accept it. However, since we are on this topic, I should like to add that unemployment seems to have become the normal state of affairs in Canada, that the number of unemployed is going up and that far from improving, things seem to be getting worse. That puts some of the people concerned in a spirit of revolt which could well lead to a national catastrophe.
I would therefore suggest that the government acknowledge that Canada's public enemy No. 1 is the present unemployment which is the cause of all this, that a state of emergency be declared and that war be waged against this menace which is threatening our country right now.
Some may say that those are drastic means, but to settle such a problem as this, I do not think that the people of Canada shall cease from considering this government responsible for the administration of the country and that it is its responsibility to take drastic means to resolve the problems that face this nation.
Mr. Chairman, I am aware that my time is almost ended, but I wish to thank the members of the house for their kind attention. We now have a democratic government in the true meaning of the word. We were elected in a democratic way. The house as it is composed gives the best picture of democracy we could have, but when a government holds 200 seats out of 265, democracy is no longer existing because the government becomes a dictatorship in such conditions. I believe that we can draw a certain advantage from the present composition of the house. We are here to work, not in the interest of political parties but in the best interests of the Canadian nation.
Ways and Means

speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member, but his time is up.

Would the hon. member allow a question? The hon. member talked about bilingualism. Does he want the leader of his own party, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) to speak both official languages fluently?

I am happy to answer that question for the member for Bonavista-Twillingate and I congratulate him for his excellent French.
I can assure him of one thing, and it is that our leader, the hon. member for Red Deer is learning French. We had an opportunity to talk French with him, and he understands the language and is making some progress; he shows good will and above all sincerity. I wish to thank and commend him. (Text):

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am rising to ask a question under the same privilege that was granted to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In view of the hon. member's commendable interest in bilingualism, I wonder whether he would explain why a recent publication of the Social Credit party is available only in French.
(Translation):
Unless I am mistaken, the hon. member is asking why some of our own publications are in English?
In French only.

As far as I know, our publications are issued in both French and English. This may not be true of some documents, and I admit that we are not 100 per cent perfect, but we are trying to improve, and I would suggest that all other members do the same.

Mr. Chairman, it is not without some misgivings that I take part for the first time in the debates of this respectable assembly.
As a new member, I find it difficult to speak on the budget without a budget having being submitted, and, Mr. Chairman, it will be realized that this will be even more difficult if I am to abide by the standing orders.
As a Canadian of Polish extraction, my first statement will be the following:	I
sincerely believe in bilingualism and national

Ways and Means
unity, as has been advocated for years by the Liberal party.
Mr. Chairman, mine is the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle, which recalls the names of two illustrious explorers in the history of Canada.
My constituency, located at the western limit of the island of Montreal, covers a third of the island. It has a population of 162,000, of which 86,000 are voters. I believe that my constituency comes fourth in Canada as regards the number of voters.
(Text):
I should like to take this occasion, Mr. Chairman, to thank the electors of the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle for the confidence they have shown in me by electing me as their representative in this house. Scattered within the boundaries of the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle we have 17 municipalities and within these municipalities we have residential, commercial, industrial and agricultural areas with enough acreage for the world's fair, the new C.B.C. headquarters and thousands of acres for other future projects.
Most of the constituency is surrounded by water, the beautiful Lachine rapids, riviere des Prairies, lake St. Louis and lake of Two Mountains, which make up part of the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa rivers. It is a sad situation when in this scientific age we let such beauty be used as a cesspool. Most of the municipalities dump their sewage directly into these lakes without any treatment.
In 1960 the government amended the National Housing Act to provide financial aid to municipalities intending to build sewage treatment plants within a certain time limit, March 31, 1963. I was happy to hear today the announcement by the Minister of Public Works in which he asked the house to approve the extension of the date to March 31, 1965. This is what I have been asking for. In fact, I have just removed four pages from my speech because of this announcement.
My predecessor, who was a Conservative and still is a Conservative and also mayor of Dorval, spoke in the debate on Bill No. C-42 which amended the National Housing Act to provide financial aid to municipalities wishing to construct and complete sewage treatment plants before March 31, 1963. As found on page 155 of Hansard of November 24, 1960, he said:
My own city of Dorval adopted a resolution to take advantage of this offer on the very night the announcement was made in the speech from the throne.
This was stated on November 24, 1960, nearly two years ago, and the city of Dorval is not ready to go ahead with their project. Their plans were not ready two months ago

and I am not sure if they are ready to proceed even now. There are many municipalities which are not ready, and which have just started preliminary study of sewage treatment projects. This date change, when approved by the house, will be good news to all municipalities across Canada, and especially to the municipalities in the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle.
As to the budget, the Conservative government has been permitted by its supporters to introduce six straight deficit budgets in a row. At present, as I understand it, this debate is a budget debate, a debate on the budget which was introduced by the past minister of finance and which the house did not have an opportunity to debate fully because the Prime Minister dissolved parliament. Now, with certain austerity measures introduced, we have a more or less revised budget or, as they call it, revised estimates introduced by the new Minister of Finance who is treated as a hero by his party because he is cutting out some of the deficit. He is still however introducing a revised deficit budget, which is not actually a budget, and therefore we have no say as to confidence in the government in matters of finance.
Mr. Chairman, I was elected in 1951 as alderman of the city of Lachine. I was in office from 1951 to 1955, and then from 1957 to date. We in municipal governments are obliged to present proper, approved, balanced budgets before we have the right to tax the people, and I am proud to announce that while I was in council we were obliged to balance our budget, we never had a deficit, and always had a surplus. In fact our director of finance, Mr. Rene Laberge, a very capable man, has had 26 surpluses in a row and has received many citations for his endeavours in municipal finance. I may add that this gentleman, in 1962, will have served the city of Lachine for 40 years.
Mr. Laberge is consulted by many town managers across Canada and in the United States regarding financial problems and management and, if you will permit me, Mr. Chairman, I would like to suggest to ministers of finance, both past and present, that they consult experts who have proper public experience, such as Mr. Laberge.
The constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle is considered the crossroads of the province of Quebec. Within our territory we have the Montreal international airport at Dorval and the C.N.R. newly constructed humpyard in Lachine, which were important Liberal projects. We also have the old Lachine canal and other government departments such as the R.C.N. naval depot at La Salle and the Pulp & Paper Research Laboratory of Canada at Pointe Claire, which were also Liberal pro-

jects. In addition we have a veterans hospital at Ste. Anne de Bellevue, many post offices, and one county unemployment insurance office in Lachine which has been busier in the past five years than ever before because of the unemployment problem which we have suffered during the past five years of Conservative government. In fact I am sure there were more withdrawals than deposits during that period, and the only visible new work seen by the unemployed was an increase in the staff of the unemployment offices.
The constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle is very heavily industrialized. We have heavy industry and light manufactures of all sorts, and the constituents are farmers, labourers, technical men, white collar workers, professional people, and businessmen. I was amazed to hear during the past five years of the large number of people collecting unemployment insurance, many of whom were white collar workers. As has been said many times, when unemployment hits the white collar workers, the situation is serious. It was serious in this county for the past five years and we see no hope of any long range improvement as a result of measures implemented by the Conservative government.
I should now like to direct special attention to the taxi and parking situation at Dorval airport and the choosing of the world's fair site on the island of Montreal. At Montreal international airport at Dorval the Department of Transport operates a metered parking lot which has a charge of 50 cents per hour, while in competition to this D.O.T. metered parking lot, and adjoining it, is a parking concession which is rented out by D.O.T. to a private concern that charges less for parking than the D.O.T. lot. In fact the concessionaires charge only 25 cents for the first two hours and 25 cents for each additional four hours, or a maximum of $1.50 per day. This means that for 50 cents at the D.O.T. lot one may park for one hour while for the same price he may park in the concession lot for six hours.
The most serious situation, however, is that when a person overparks his car on the D.O.T. parking lot it is towed away and he is compelled to pay an additional charge of $2 plus costs. On summary conviction a fine of up to $50 may be imposed by the courts. This tends to force all airport customers and visitors to park on the concession lot, which is cheaper, rather than on the D.O.T. metered parking lot. Such a situation is detrimental to Department of Transport operations and profits. It is also detrimental to the good name of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police because they are being used to enforce these unjustified regulations which force airport customers to use the concession 27507-3-79}
Ways and Means
parking lot, rather than the D.O.T. parking lot which is more expensive and has very strict regulations.
It seems that all these regulations are designed to bring profit to the concessionaires rather than to bring about proper operations. If you, sir, will permit me to go further, then I say the population of the island of Montreal is deprived of proper services to and from the airport through these regulations, and this is done in order to protect a few individuals who own and operate concessions at the airport.
No one can enter the airport unless he goes by private car, taxi or special bus, and in nearly every case the concessionaires will make a profit. No commuter buses, such as the Montreal transportation commission buses and the provincial transport buses, which together service the whole island of Montreal, have the right to enter the airport grounds, and therefore the population of the island of Montreal is deprived of proper transit service to and from the airport.
There are two other concessions which are not justified. These are the special taxi, or limousine service as some call it, and the special bus service which operates from the hotel area to the airport. No taxi has the right to pick up a passenger at the airport unless specially called by that passenger. Indeed many taxi owners have been taken to court for this offence and have been condemned to pay heavy fines. I say to the committee, open the airport to all taxis under special licences or permits and allow the Montreal transportation commission's services to be extended to the airport so as to give full and proper service to and from the airport to all the population in the vicinity of it. I also say that the Department of Transport should operate all parking facilities without regimentation and at a lower charge.
Having received so many complaints about these injustices I could even go as far as to say that the reason why there is no drinking fountain on the main floor of the administration building is that the concessionnaires will sell more soft drinks. This is how far this government and their directorate have gone.
Mr. Chairman, the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle, has thousands of acres of vacant land available, four main highways including the trans-Canada highway, the two main railways of Canada and the airways of the world passing through this constituency. Where else but here can the Canadian government choose a site for the world's fair and even the new headquarters of the C.B.C.? It would be a waste of public money if the Canadian government were to decide to expropriate land in the centre of the city of

Ways and Means
Montreal, where there are no proper parking facilities, where there is a serious confusion of traffic problems which have no solution, and where expropriation of built up areas would cost the Canadian people millions of extra dollars. This waste is unnecessary, when the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle has available all this vacant land in the proper locations. In fact, if the government while promoting an austerity program wastes public funds unnecessarily, then the people, the public, will be very suspicious of this government as to their real intentions regarding saving, austerity, and of their sincerity.
Mr. Chairman, I have noticed with interest the public works developments going on at this moment in the vicinity of Confederation Heights within the outskirts of Ottawa. Here you have the new headquarters for the Post Office Department, the C.B.C. and many other departments. The constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle has many sites similar to the one at Confederation Heights; therefore there is no need for the federal government to waste money on the expropriation of built up areas in Montreal when we have so much open land in the constituency of Jacques Cartier-Lasalle, where proper sites for the world's fair, the C.B.C. and other federal projects could easily be found.

Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege to extend to the Minister of Finance, the Hon. George Nowlan, congratulations and best wishes in his new portfolio. The province of Nova Scotia has given to the public service of Canada many men and women of distinction and ability. None of these have earned a greater measure of respect and admiration than our colleague in his capacity as minister of national revenue. In the same spirit I am reminded of those sterling qualities which the former minister of finance, now the Minister of Justice, brought to bear in the discharge of his duties. History will record that he worked as one inspired at a time when this nation faced great and searching problems, most of which had been shelved by the former administration for more than ten years. After 22 years of Liberal rule the people of this nation faced the prospect of foreign domination and control of our resources both industrial and financial. The hon. member for Eglinton in his capacity as minister of finance never lost sight of the greater Canada that should be the objective of all Canadians. Those engaged in the primary industries of agriculture, labour and manufacturing will forever owe a measure of gratitude and appreciation for his resourceful years as Canada's minister of finance.
During the past several years this government, led by the Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, has instituted long term policies which step by step are ensuring that Canadians can and will recapture that measure of equity and control which was so lavishly and unashamedly surrendered to outside interests by the former government in the late years of that administration. Opposition members in this debate have glibly talked of what they would do to regain the control of our resources. A few years ago their boast was that Canadians were allowing outside interests, particularly from the United States, to take over an increasing control of many of our natural resources. That was one of the great boasts of that administration, the extent to which foreign capital was taking over the resources of our country, and their apathy to the most vital of our resources-I refer to our human resources-was not the least of their sins.
Where was the long term policy then? Their boast in those days was. "You never had it better". For a short-time popularity they squandered a great part of the Canadian heritage and the consequences of their folly should, I believe, remind them of the adage that there are none so blind as those who begin to believe their own propaganda. I would recommend that adage to the hon. member for Essex West. He might profitably consider that for a moment or two. After listening to his discourse I have come to the conclusion that he is a new Liberal, and I emphasize the word "new". He must have been listening to the hon. member for Davenport and the hon. member for Essex East. In fact, I think they must have been writing history for him, because they did not tell him how the Liberals lived with the exchange crisis of 1947 and 1948. That cannot absolve him from the knowledge of the arrogance and neglect of 1956 and 1957. The tarnish of those days cannot be easily forgotten.
Who said that the Atlantic region should be vacated? I would like to say that he sits over there today, but he is absent, as he has been so many times during the last several weeks. What was the long term policy of those who said, "If they want our wheat, let them come and get it"? Who left the western farmer to smother under the surpluses so arrogantly accumulated? Who today is the champion of that sordid heritage; who but the newest thing in the Liberal party, the hon. member for Assiniboia, who also is not in his seat at the present moment?
On a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman, I was talking to Your Honour. I am in the chamber.

Mr. Chairman, I acknowledge that the hon. member is now in his seat; and he is a good looking gentleman, I will say that. The hon. member lor Essex West has something to say about Canada's unemployed. Who failed to provide training for Canadians entering the labour market? Who failed to consider the case of those caught by automation? Who left Canadian businessmen to fend for themselves-
John; Dief.

-in the face of competition from companies who owed their loyalty and control to head offices outside Canada? All this, when their boast was that we had a budget surplus. That is the real history of neglect, arrogance and political deceit, the only answer Canadians can find in the Liberal party today. These are the people who have charged this government with fraud and deceit of the Canadian people. These self-confessed accusers sought to win an election. Talk of dirty linen, the whispered word, the naked assassination of character, frustration gleaming like an evil genius in a truth as often half told as left untold;-
What is the hon. member reading from?
-shame fleeing unashamedly into the inner recesses of some ambitious mind. None but a few can claim and own the conscience that tolerates that kind and style-
Straight from the heart.
-of authorship and purpose. There was no price they would not pay to win their way to power.
I think Senator Grosart wrote that.

They have earned a just reward-a minor and diminishing role in a divided opposition.
There is no satisfaction in mentioning these things, but I believe the Liberals in my constituency would want me to satisfy the record. Some of them will remember the first speech I ever made. That was many years ago, in a public school oratory contest. My topic was the life of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, that great Canadian and Liberal statesman. I believe the Liberals of Rosthern constituency and the Liberals across Canada would agree that were Sir Wilfrid alive today he would not have endorsed the kind of campaign which had the blessing of the Leader of the Opposition during the last election campaign. He knew you could not build a nation by trying to destroy your political opponents. So it is in Canada today. Canada needs a strong government. Canada needs a stronger opposition
Ways and Means
than we find in this parliament. Those who glory in the fact that we have a minority government can also take credit for the fact that we have a divided opposition. I, for one, do not consider this situation as one to be continued for any length of time. The urgency and immediate purpose of the legislative program before us as set out in the speech from the throne this fall and in the budget last spring, cannot be denied.
I wish to make some reference, for the benefit of some of the new members of this house and, in particular, for the benefit of the hon. member for Fraser Valley, to the program which was embarked upon five years ago and which has received revision and reconsideration in the intervening period. I would point out, particularly to members of the Social Credit group, that the measures now brought to the attention of the house are further refinements of existing legislation which has been brought in in the past, as a result of experience gained during the past several years. I can think of some things which have been done since 1957, and it is a matter of record that most of those things have been endorsed in the House of Commons by members of the opposition. There were one or two occasions on which they took a stand which was somewhat different, but by and large they supported what was done, though in an apologetic way which has endeared them to our hearts.
I think of the National Housing Act and of the thousands of Canadians who were able to build homes for their families during the years when they needed those homes. These Canadians know what the deficit did for them, as also do the thousands of seasonal workers who were employed in the building of those homes.
I think of the amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and what they have done for those who have been seasonally unemployed.
I think of the increases in the pensions to members of the civil service, the armed forces and the R.C.M.P. I ask hon. members to consider this: what segment of our labour community enjoys greater security and employment benefits than these?
I think of the improved benefits made available under the Veterans Insurance Act, the Returned Soldiers' Insurance Act and the Children of War Dead (Education Assistance) Act.
I think of the amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and of the implementation of the Prairie Grain Advance Payment Act, together with the provision of acreage payments.

Ways and Means
The last increase was made by a Liberal government.
That is not altogether true.
It is 100 per cent true.
The amendments brought in by this party during the last parliament extended the benefits of P.F.A.A. to a greater number of people than ever before.
But did not increase the amount of payment.

I think of the Farm Credit Corporation and the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and the millions of additional money authorized to help individual farm families develop a healthy agricultural industry. I think of the increased amounts voted under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, the millions of dollars expended to support and maintain the price of dairy products in central and maritime Canada, and the further substantial subsidies allowed on the movement of grain on behalf of feeders and farmers in central and maritime Canada.
What about the cent a dozen for eggs?
What about the peanuts?

I think of the development assistance given Saskatchewan, for the South Saskatchewan river dam and the moneys voted for harbour improvements at Churchill, on Hudson Bay, and on both coasts, as well as along the St. Lawrence river waterway. I think of the increased assistance given our universities and students attending universities. I think of the assistance provided to our municipalities-and this has been further illustrated today-at a time when such assistance was most timely, due to the changing complexion of community life in Canada. I think of the revision of the Estate Tax Act the Income Tax Act and the increased exemptions under the Excise Tax Act. I think of the Queen Elizabeth fund for research into the diseases of children. I think of the increased use of the Export Credits Insurance Act, and all that it has meant to our exporters by way of trade.
I think of the municipal winter works incentive program which has continued to expand each year since it was established.
I think of all the provisions which have been made for training our unemployed, those human resources all but forgotten by the former Liberal administration. I think of the establishment of the new Department of Forestry in recognition of the importance of this segment of our economy.
Are you getting this one reprinted?
It is printed already.
I think of the accelerated depreciation allowances provided to assist new industries in areas having substantial employment problems.
Read on.

I think of the encouragement given by direct assistance to fishermen and to the fishing and shipbuilding industries of this nation. I think of the program ARDA, which was attacked by the hon. member for Assiniboia, a program which will give to communities in central and maritime Canada help which they never got from the Liberal government.
More pilot projects.

I think of the legislation approved to provide rail services to remote resource areas of our nation. I think of the development which is already following the roads to resources program which was laughed at by members of the Liberal party when it was brought before this house. I think of the action which was taken to oblige foreign companies to divulge their operations for scrutiny. I think of the encouragement given to the utilization of Canadian executive talent in the composition of foreign companies set up in Canada. I think of the encouragement given to the people of other countries to settle in Canada to practice their trades. I think of the igloo to igloo mentality of the opposition, pitifully and precariously trying to ride the fence in every one of the debates leading to these achievements. If the people of Toronto could have seen the hon. member for Davenport riding that fence the other day they would have had reason to ask: where is this new Liberal party of which we heard so much during the election campaign?
Where is the Tory member for Davenport?
Where is the Liberal member for Davenport, whom we hardly ever see in this House of Commons?
Most of the defeated Tories are back on the payroll.

To all these actions, hon. members opposite respond with the tired, ostrich inspired platitudes that fall so naturally from the lips of opposition speakers. That is the weakness of our opposition today. The quarrel in this parliament is not with the government. The quarrel or, more properly, the struggle, is with the other opposition parties in this parliament. Their difficulty and,

I believe, their nagging concern is: who will really emerge as the official opposition in this parliament?
You will.
No doubt about that.

The hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate says: "No doubt about that". A few more seats gained during the last election cannot fail to affect the thinking in that party by the remnant of those who sit-
Remnant?
-that remnant whose arrogance is greater than the arrogance they showed during the last period when they were in power.
You should have rehearsed it once more before coming in.

Before resuming my seat I have a few observations I should like to make and place before the minister and the government in regard to matters which might be taken into consideration, and which I believe may affect the welfare of the people in my constituency.
You have finished the Grosart part of your speech. Now get on with your own.
I would venture the opinion that this parliament should not underestimate the Canadian people-
