speechtext: Mr. Chairman, our chameleonlike friend over there from Assiniboia has been sitting in his place and consistently, persistently and rudely, and in an unparliamentary way, making interjections unworthy of him, and I would ask that he desist.

Mr. Chairman, the record will show that on almost every occasion on which I have spoken in this session I have had innumerable interruptions from hon. members opposite about which I made no complaint to the Chair.

Mr. Chairman, Canadians cannot hope to regain the control and ownership of their resource industries without some effort and sacrifice, and I am one of those who believe that the people of this country want to share to a wider degree than most of our political parties want to think they
Ways and Means
do in the building of a greater Canada. The nations of the world are reorganizing their trading patterns, and this will affect the course that Canada must follow. The industrial potential of Europe does not allow for a very substantial or successful entry of Canadian industrial products into the market. We will be hard put to maintain our traditional markets. There is a market in other parts of the world, but it is not readily available to us on a cash basis. I do not believe that any tangible benefits will accrue to Canada by way of any substantial program for the disposition of our production as gifts. There is, however, a great need for heavy industrial machinery in almost every one of these developing areas. There is also an ample labour supply in almost every one of these developing areas, and many of these nations are well supplied with some of the raw materials they require.
The problems to be met and overcome are considerable. However, I believe that we should be giving them more thought than has hitherto been given to them, and that we should look upon these areas as areas of opportunity for the expansion and the development of our own trading potential. The future of Canada's position in the trading world certainly to my mind does not lie in Europe alone, except in so far as raw materials are concerned. Here at home one of the evils of our society is the cost of consumer credit. There is a need for the mobilization of more economical credit facilities than are available through the ordinary finance companies. I believe that our credit unions and caisse populaires could be given greater encouragement. These associations are controlled by local people, and I believe they could be of great assistance to the country in the government's over-all program to restore Canadian ownership and control of our resources. There are areas of service where privately owned enterprise has failed to supply the need. Co-operative effort by the people in these communities might very well be the only remaining answer. I believe that at a time like this, when the free world finds herself confronted by the advocates of socialism and communism, we must utilize every resource at our disposal to meet the type of competition they pose. Therefore, I would propose that consideration be given to the establishment of a department of cooperatives at the federal level.
Canada will continue to grow and prosper despite the mutterings of the opposition. During the next several years our economy will reach new levels of prosperity and achievement. The long term policies brought into effect during the past five years will ensure that increasing numbers of Canadians will

Ways and Means
share the fruits of prosperity. There will always be an opposition in parliament. For the sake of Canada, let us hope that it will be stronger than the present one, particularly in the sense that healthy, constructive opposition is one of the bulwarks and safeguards of our democracy. I pity those few in the opposition whose bitterness knows no bounds. A few years at the most is left to them, and this is more than they deserve. After all, abuse is no substitute for criticism.
I should like to thank the hon. member for Essex East-and I am sorry he is not in the committee today either-for his efforts on my behalf during the recent election campaign. I assure him and the members of his party that had they consulted me we could have provided them with more people than turned out to the hon. member's meeting in my riding during the campaign. Canadians will remember the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. Let us hope and pray that they will forgive them as well. In the meantime, Canada can go ahead to new achievements under the leadership of the Prime Minister, the Eight Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, who serves the national purpose of all Canadians.

Mr. Chairman, I am very glad to be able to rise in this house and put forward my views on the revised estimates brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Nowlan). I suggest that this budget is one of the most important items of the current session.
Mr. Chairman, I shall try to be as short as possible.
I am perhaps not as much of an orator as certain politicians who have been in this house for many years and who have always been misunderstood because their speeches carried too many words and too few solutions.
Mr. Chairman, having heard the remarks of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Che-vrier), the other evening, and those of the member for Dollard (Mr. Rouleau) this morning, I cannot imagine how these men, with all their experience with Liberal policies, and after having deceived the people so often with their election promises, still dare to get up in this house and try to have us accept a solution to cope with the problems which we are now facing, while they have never been able to solve them when they were in power.
As has already been said, our hon. friends from the Liberal party are very strong while
[Mr. Nasserden.l
in opposition, but when they are in office, they become completely helpless for want of responsible policies.
Mr. Chairman, were not our Liberal friends in office during the years 1935-39-
Tell us something about the Conservatives.

-when they were spending thousands and thousands of dollars abroad, although we were starving in Canada, on the pretence of erecting a statue which would bring independence to Canada in case of another war.
After having criticized the previous Conservative government, and rightly so, I suggest, since the Conservatives were in power during the first world war, our Liberal friends did exactly the same thing, but in a more hypocritical way.
Then, they had us accept restrictions, rationing and conscription. They asked us to sacrifice our brothers, they tore the hearts of our mothers, and they had us sacrifice our time and our money-in a very hypocritical way, I repeat-under pretence of paving the way for prosperity after the war. The same Liberals who were in power at that time come back today with an over-all planning policy.
We are not the people in power.

Mr. Chairman, during the last election, I was honoured by a visit of the hon. member for Laurier in my riding. He came to give his clown act several times and in several places in the province of Quebec, and he helped-I must thank him for it-the election of 26 Social Crediters.
What about your leader, Mr. Caouette?

In order to have lively meetings, the hon. member had to rely on the officials of the provincial government and beg them to hold joint meetings, otherwise he would have had to speak before an almost empty house.
Mr. Chairman, I know that within the Liberal party there are men of great intelligence and understanding who, unfortunately, have to bow before the dictatorship of three or four politicians whom I do not need to mention.
Mr. Chairman, I am not here to praise the Conservative party but I want to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar.

In 1956, when the Liberals were defeated, credit restrictions had been put into effect by the government in power to the point of even stopping loans for home construction. The contractors who, in previous years, had been able to build homes were forced to lay off their workers as they had no more work for them.
Mr. Chairman, in 1957, the Conservative party again provided the contractors with funds with some restrictions, of course, and created a system which, though not perfect, did at least help fight unemployment. The government encouraged us to undertake winter works, even if they were not acceptable and were far from profitable for the builders.
I represent the riding of Levis which is blessed with the largest and the most up to date shipyards in Canada, employing a great number of workers in my riding and in the area. During the years I mentioned and when our Liberal friends were in power, there were lots of ships being built. It was during the war, of course, since, with the Liberals, prosperity only comes in times of war.
My opponent at the polls was a man who represented the riding during 22 years.
He did a fine job of it.

When the Liberals met with opposition, they demanded that an able man be appointed to a key position within the cabinet, a thing they never did while they were in power. That is further evidence of the fact that they can do anything when they are in the opposition.
In my opinion, it would be a good thing if the present government were to take steps to guarantee the employment of our workers so that the latter may give their families a decent standard of living. Since our shipyards are not an ordinary industry, the government should maintain the present subsidy and even increase it to encourage private companies to have their merchant ships built in Canada.
The government should always have ships to build in order to secure jobs for at least 2,500 workers, thus providing work to our people all year round.
I feel this would contribute materially to improve the unemployment situation. We have been deploring for too long in my riding that workers are employed for three to six months a year. How can you expect a head of family to have confidence in his
Ways and Means
elected representatives when he never knows whether he will have a job the next day or the next week?
I have the honour to represent a riding which supported the Liberals for 22 years, but which was nevertheless neglected for quite a long time. There are a great deal of public works to be carried out, such as the building of post offices and bridges, improvement of the trans-Canada highway and several other works that were left undone. As a matter of fact, we do not even have a proper road leading to a wharf built under the Liberal administration.
The present government should correct the mistakes of the previous governments and start immediately. We also urgently need a bridge or a tunnel to join the south shore and Quebec city.
In my opinion, the government should take that responsibility, since in my experience a company cannot carry out the work economically at the present rates of interest. The federal government only, with the co-operation of the provincial government, will be able to issue capital by using the Bank of Canada. I know that the tunnel or the bridge will be economically sound and that the revenues will be high enough to pay off the capital, but not the interest. With the present monetary system we would have to pay three times the capital.
We also have several work requests, including one that has already been submitted to the government.
It has to do with the building of a wall along the St. Lawrence river, in the eastern and western sections of the city of Lauzon, in Levis, St. Romuald and St. David, to protect the waterfront property owners against damages often caused by the high tides of the beautiful St. Lawrence river.
In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, the few suggestions I have just made should be examined in relation to the current estimates as a means of helping our unemployed and providing some breathing space in our unemployment offices.
I also believe that, in addition to promoting winter works, this government should accept-again in co-operation with provincial and municipal governments, so as not to deprive them of their autonomy-to pay part of the cost of the material through the grants already provided for.
That would be of great assistance to prevent the municipalities from building up the deficits they suffer each year in trying to

Mr. Chairman, in rising to take part in this very strange debate, this budget debate without a budget, I cannot help but think that this really reflects the hand of the inimitable former minister of finance who argued so strongly in the house a couple of weeks ago to prove that we should save a six day budget debate if it took us six weeks to do so. This debate has to do with the economic good or ills of our country. It started last year before the previous parliament was dissolved and it has been resumed under quite different circumstances. If we cast our eyes around the chamber we see a lot of new faces. I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs mentioned one day that all the new members in the house this time represented a cross section of the people. I would suggest that

they were a very cross section of the people, a little more cross in some areas than they were in others.
However, I believe there is one thing that is very significant about this new house and that is the division in the group across the floor from us at the present time. It really consists of two groups, the western Socreds and the eastern Socreds. With regard to the western Socreds, I have always found it very difficult to distinguish a Social Crediter from Alberta from a Tory from Alberta. They always seemed to vote the same way and they still do. They seem to share the same views, including the view that we should sell Canada to the United States as fast as possible. In fact, Mr. Chairman, that seems to be the parchment on which the present marriage licence between the two is written.
We also have a new group consisting of the Social Credit members from the province of Quebec, the province in which I was born and raised. I think that this is a direct result of our present economic situation. In the newspaper Le Devoir of recent date there was a short comment which I think is very appropriate. They were discussing possible realignments in the house and this is what they had to say:
If some day there is some realignment of parties, it will be done in some other way. The Liberals and Conservatives, excepting some individuals in both groups, will be destined definitely to join their forces, because there is nothing of a practical nature which separates them.
I think that is very true, Mr. Chairman, and in my opinion the truth of that statement has never been demonstrated any better than in the great province of Quebec. At this time I should like to congratulate the province of Quebec on finally, for the first time in 100 years, breaking the yoke of the two old parties by which that province has been held for so long a time. This yoke has led to many things and the efforts to break away from it have been demonstrated in recent years. I believe this is one of the causes of the separatist movement in the province of Quebec which in my view is very easy to understand. I believe that Canadians living in any other province would feel like separating themselves from a country where they felt like foreigners when they travelled to another province in that country. I think this is the feeling that led to this movement in the province of Quebec. After all, our French Canadian brothers were among the first settlers of this great country and if when they travel from their own province to another they feel that they are treated at least as badly as, if not worse than

foreigners entering the country, then there is certainly great reason for them to be discontented.
In my view the forces that are responsible for this basic unrest had champions in equal numbers in both of the old line parties in this house over the years. I recall that when a friend of mine in the trade union movement visited Montreal some few years ago he was introduced to the late premier of that province, Mr. Duplessis. The introduction took place in the lobby of a hotel where the premier was about to address a convention of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. When my friend was introduced to the premier he asked him if he was going to tell the delegates how they could further exploit the French Canadians. The late premier was very incensed, of course, until my friend pointed out that at the back of the convention hall there were signs outlining the advantages to industry of moving to the province of Quebec and among the advantages was low wages. In other words, the invitation was there, as my friend said, to come to that province and exploit the French Canadians. Therefore I am rather pleased that the province of Quebec is finally on the move, though it is regrettable that the first move they should make is a backward one instead of a forward one. However, I think that will straighten itself out in good time.
There is something else that intrigues me which is common to the other three parties in this house. They decry the New Democrats as being socialistic, as though this was some terrible horror against which they were trying to warn the Canadian people. Yet what do we see? Let us take our friends opposite first. The three main things that the Social Crediters cry for are an increase in old age pensions, an increase in family allowances and the curbing of the finance companies. I should like to know just what kind of free enterprise measures those are. If they really believe in this great free enterprise about which they talk, surely these would not be the three most important things they would put forward.
Let us take a look at our friends in the other corner, the Liberals. What do we hear mostly from them?
You are the ones in a corner. We are not in a corner.

I hear some of the Liberal members saying that they are not in a corner.
There is one thing the Minister of Justice is prone to do and which I fully intend to check him on when he does it again. He refers to opinions expressed on his side of the
Ways and Means
house, but I would like to remind him that he should refer to his corner of the house because, under the present situation, we all have a corner we can talk about.
Health insurance and portable pensions are the favorite subjects of the Liberals at the moment, but it would be very hard to classify them as free enterprise subjects. I was only two years old when the Liberals first started promising us health insurance and I do not see any more reason to believe them now than I did then. In fact, Mr. Chairman, the Liberals are the real progressive conservatives; they are progressive when in opposition and utterly conservative when in power.
I now turn to our friends on the government side of the house. What measures has the government introduced during the past five years which were successful? I can list a few of them. They include the roads to resources program, the winter works program, the National Housing Act, the Farm Credit Act, ARDA and others, and I should like to say a few words about these programs.
Last summer I had the pleasure of attending the opening of highway 101 in my constituency. It links Porcupine Camp with the Sault Ste. Marie area and the last 60 miles of the road, the final link-up between Timmins and Chapleau, was built under the roads to resources program, with the federal government putting up 50 per cent of the cost of construction. When complimenting the government for this project I should like to apologize to it at the same time for my local chamber of commerce. At the official opening, which followed the June election by about five days, a great effort was made to show that this road was a straight and direct gift from the Ontario provincial government. All the provincial Ontario Conservative officials for miles around were brought there and paraded back and forth, and not a single mention was made of the fact that the federal government had contributed 50 per cent of the cost of the road. While I apologize for that, I hope that ignorant display on the part of my own local chamber of commerce will not influence any decisions the government might make with regard to other projects in the area.
It may be possible to understand some of the reasons for it. After all, as I say, it was only five days after the election and I am sure the Conservatives in the north country needed something to boost their morale.
I should like to congratulate the Minister of Public Works on the announcement he made today with regard to the extension of the time limit for sewer programs and so forth. The deadline has been extended from March, 1963, to March 31, 1965 and this is

Ways and Means
of particular importance to the region I represent because, like so many other parts of Canada, we have very severe winters and, when March 31 comes along, while it may mean something to southern parts of Canada, certainly the north is still in the middle of the deep freeze.
I had occasion during the noon hour to be speaking with the city clerk of my home town and I can assure the minister a great deal of pleasure was expressed by officials of the town of Timmins at his decision to extend the time limit, because it means they can now go ahead with very much needed and worth-while projects.
There is a lesson to be learned by all these programs which were successfully launched by the government over the past five years, and the lesson is that it is only when government takes the lead that we can meet, or take steps to meet, some of the problems of our day. Even the well publicized program and activities of the Minister of Trade and Commerce illustrate and underline the same point. There is a big hullabaloo about how he is building up markets around the world, but why should we feel surprised at that? Is not that his job? The only reason we lost a lot of these markets was because the previous government did not do its job. It left these things entirely in the hands of a few greedy individuals who sold us down the river, and we found that the traditional markets, which we hoped would be ours for all time, were being cut into by other people. It is certainly high time the government took a lead in this field, but I would like the government to use a little bit more integrity when discussing such things.
We do not mind the government using our ideas. If hon. members look at some of the successful programs I have mentioned they will find that they had been advocated for many years by people in this group. Therefore we do not mind the government using our ideas; but while it is implementing them it should not try to scare the people away from them. How can anyone hope for success under such circumstances? I say to the government, do not bite the hand that feeds you; do not try to make people afraid of the measures you hope are really going to work. Further than that, I say to the spokesmen of the three other parties, when they are discussing these so-called socialistic measures they should not substitute virulent abuse for argument.
If the programs we advocate work and are successful, then in heaven's name let us expand them. Let us encourage them. Let us even try new programs and new ideas, because the ideas which are being implemented

today were in themselves brand new ideas a few years ago. We should remember that history shows us that the problems of the world, including Canada's problems, arise must faster than we can ever cope with them.
In closing, I compliment the government on the few steps it has taken in the right direction, and I call on it to broaden out those steps.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend by taking part in this debate to unduly delay its conclusion. However, as it is customary in the course of such debates to talk about one's own constituency, I will take a few minutes of the time of the house to mention one of the serious problems in my district.
To really understand and set this problem in its true light, one must divide my constituents into three classes:
In the first place, the farmers make up over 50 per cent of the population. The other day I had the opportunity of expressing my views on the Farm Credit Act and that is why I shall not dwell at too much length on that class of people.
In the second place the small industrialists established almost everywhere in the villages of my county and trying by all possible means to survive.
However, there is a grave problem facing them. They lack the credit to face the competition of large industry. I would like the government to make credit somewhat more easily available so that they may earn a livelihood and remain in their chosen profession: manufacturers able to compete with large industry.
In the third place, the lumberjacks. These people are about the most forelorn in my constituency.
Some of them earn their living working in the woods or in the state of Maine, others go to Ontario. It is the only way for them to carry out their trade.
I would like to insist on the problems involved in this trade. Those in the first group, who go to Maine, live in the north of my constituency. They work six or seven months a year, during the period when bark is removed from the logs and they are without work for the rest of the year, which goes to say that they live off their earnings of six or seven months.
During the five or six months they are out of work, they are faced with serious financial problems to manage to provide for the needs of their families.

Those people are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits since they do not work in Canada. The state of Maine does not give them any assistance whatsoever because they are not American citizens.
I feel that the government is unfair toward these people and that the unemployment insurance commission, having been established to help all classes of citizens, should not rule out those lumbermen who go to work in Maine, because it deprives them, so to speak, of the right to live like all other Canadians.
I urge the government to start negotiations with the authorities of that state with a view to coming to an agreement and implementing legislation to make those lumbermen eligible for unemployment insurance benefits during the months they are out of work.
If that arrangement were made, all Canadian workers would find themselves on an equal basis and would be entitled to benefit by the legislation enacted by the government to help workers during the unemployment season.
That anomaly should be corrected immediately and maybe the lumbermen would show their appreciation to the government for solving their problem.
In any trade, whether a man is a garage mechanic, a baker, a salesman, etc., he is entitled to deduct from his income tax the price of the tools he needs in his trade.
The anomaly here, as I see it, is that people engaged in wood cutting are entitled to deduct neither the price of their tools nor their travelling expenses at the beginning and at the end of the wood cutting season.
Those people should be entitled to the same exemption as the other taxpayers, that is, $1,000, for, at the present time, they can only claim one of about $600 since they have to pay almost $400 each year in equipment and travelling expenses.
Therefore, I ask the government to consider the problem of those people and to find a way of enabling them to deduct their equipment and travelling expenses from their income tax, so that they may find themselves on the same footing as all other Canadian citizens in various other trades.
To summarize, I ask the government to work out an agreement with the authorities of the state of Maine, so that lumbermen in my constituency who work there become eligible to unemployment insurance benefits. As a matter of fact, all lumbermen in Canada should be entitled to deduct the price of equipment and travelling expenses from their income tax.
Ways and Means
There are many other points I should like to bring to the attention of this house, but I shall have an opportunity to do so later. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, I do not want to take too much time so I will stop here for now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I wonder whether the committee could now agree that the general discussion has terminated and that we will go on to consider the specific resolutions before the committee, which consist of the Income Tax Act, the Estate Tax Act, and so on. Is that agreed?
Agreed.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, I would like to say a word on that, if I may.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think I could simplify this matter, Mr. Chairman. The practice has been to call each individual paragraph. Unless the committee has other views, I think that procedure would most facilitate the work of the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I am afraid my views are slightly at variance with the views expressed by the acting minister, whom I should like to congratulate on his sudden and, for most of us, rather unexpected elevation.
Surely not unexpected?

Well, if it were a matter of merit I would say it should have happened long ago. Indeed, if it were a matter of merit I may say that the country would have been a lot better off if the hon. member for Carleton had been minister of finance for the last five years rather than the gentleman who held that portfolio.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Beware of Greeks bearing gifts.
But it does bring to our minds the reflection, how are the mighty fallen, because the general experience is that when a minister is discarded, at least he becomes the acting minister.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I thought the hon. member was to be relevant.

Ways and Means

This is a preliminary
courtesy, and I have now concluded it. I do think the hon. member for Carleton, who is acting minister, would agree with me that, since about half the hon. members of the house were not here when the budget was presented and when the general scheme of taxation was laid before us by the former minister of finance, it would be helpful to the committee if we could have a very brief and thoroughly relevant discussion of the general changes in income tax and what their purport is before going on to the individual items.
I would not imagine that would take very long. I would think that if it were properly conducted it would lessen the time that would be taken on the individual paragraphs. I recall only rather vaguely the budget speech of last April, but my recollection is that there was some sort of scheme or purpose in these items, or there purported to be. I think it would be helpful to those of us who need our memory refreshed, and to those who have no memory to refresh, if the acting minister could very briefly tell us what is the general purport of these items, as one or two hon. members might wish to comment on that before we consider the individual items.

Mr. Chairman, I am in the hands of the committee in this matter. It does seem to me that we would be able to proceed more rapidly if we were to take each of the individual paragraphs, giving effect to what was the general purport and structure of the budget. If there is a general view that there should be a review, I would be willing to undertake it, although I am quite satisfied that the resolution could receive much more expeditious attention if they were called paragraph by paragraph.

Of course, the Chair realizes that, on a strict point of order, it is one resolution that is before the committee and it can only be restricted by unanimous consent. I feel it would be proper on behalf of this party to agree to a restriction by consent after a very brief general discussion, but I do think it would facilitate the debate if we were to have that first.

Perhaps I could draw the attention of the committee to a few particular measures which were outlined in the budget on April 10, 1962 commencing at page 2705 of Hansard. The budget speech at this point details the changes which were proposed in the income tax legislation. The first change, which is the one outlined in paragraph 1, is the increase in exemptions in respect of dependants by $50. The effect of this is that since 1957 the exemption in respect of dependants has been increased from
[Mr. Bell (Carleton).!
$150 to $300 for persons in receipt of family allowances, and from $400 for those not in receipt of family allowances, to a total, now, of $550. This further increase in the deductible amount results in some 80,000 taxpayers being freed completely from the payment of income tax and brings about a modest reduction for all remaining taxpayers who support dependants.
A second and central feature of the budget resolutions, was a production incentive made available to those companies engaged in manufacturing and processing. It consists of cancellation of 50 per cent of the tax on the first $50,000 of taxable income arising from increased sales, and cancellation of 25 per cent of the tax on any additional income arising from increased sales. Provision for double depreciation is continued for a further period of three years.
The third feature of this resolution deals with scientific research in industry, and for the first time the government has recommended to the house that 150 per cent of increased expenditures may be deducted in respect of scientific research undertaken for industrial purposes. It is hoped that this, in addition, to the provision which has actually been made for direct assistance through the national research council will result in a great deal more scientific research being undertaken in this country.
There are important matters having to do with the oil and gas industry, and I think I can outline them under three headings. The new proposals are, first, that individuals be granted the right to charge petroleum preproduction expenses against income earned from oil and gas production; second, that all companies including those not normally engaged in petroleum or in mining be granted the right to charge petroleum preproduction expenses against income earned from oil and gas production; and, third, that expenditures involved in the acquisition, after the date of the budget, of rights to explore or drill for oil or gas, or to extract oil or gas, be deductible under section 83A of the Income Tax Act along with other drilling and exploration expenses, and proceeds from sales of such rights be taken into income by all taxpayers, including individuals.
Then there are significant changes applying effectively to the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia with respect to logging taxes. Here it is proposed that the tax credit extended by the federal government shall be the amount of two thirds of the provincial tax up to a maximum rate of 10 per cent. As hon. members of the committee know, this was a matter which was raised at the dominion-provincial conference and was the

subject of a proposal to the provincial premiers at that time. This is a significant concession and one which has been greatly welcomed by the forest industries.
Finally, in relation to these resolutions, there is a provision for the continuation of the system whereby university grants are paid in a certain province. I should say provision is made for an alternative arrangement under which the province which wishes to administer its own grants has a deduction from corporation taxes enabling that province to pay $1.50 per capita of its population to universities, an amount which, under the terms of other legislation now on the order paper, would be raised to $2. These are the principal provisions of the budget as far as they relate to income and corporation taxes. I hope this brief review may be of some help to the committee. I shall be glad to give detailed information about the various items as we go along.

In the course of his brief remarks, the minister referred to certain amendments to the Income Tax Act which would provide concessions with respect to drilling and exploration expenses incurred by companies seeking petroleum or natural gas.
I should like at this time to place before this committee a request which was received some time ago by the Minister of Finance and by the Minister of National Revenue from the Western Peat Moss Company. This application, I believe, concerns all peat moss exploration in this country. The application was supported by a brief asking for the classification of the peat moss industry as a mining operation for the purposes of the Income Tax Act. I should like to place on record some of the points which were included in it.
In the introductory remarks, the company requested classification of the peat moss industry as a mining operation, either by recognizing that peat moss production is mining or by adding to the act a section specifically stating that the peat moss industry shall have the benefit of tax concessions similar to those enjoyed by the mining industry. I should like to draw attention to the importance of the peat moss industry in the eastern provinces- in the province of Quebec, and, particularly over the last few years, in the northeastern section of New Brunswick.
The assertion is that production operations on a peat bog, as well as exploration, surveying, drilling and preproduction, are quite comparable to similar stages in the mining industry, and that they warrant similar consideration. We know that the mining industry is granted tax concessions as a stimulant and as an incentive for the capital to accept the problems and hazards involved in developing one of the natural resources of this country. In
Ways and Means
submitting its application for the peat moss industry, this company takes the position that similar incentives with respect to that industry would be equally advantageous to Canada. The brief mentions that at present the taxation of this industry depends on local assessing practice which is not necessarily standardized. The industry submits that it requires the spelling out of specific allowances and concessions which, in my opinion, should be similar to those accorded with respect to mining operations or drilling and exploration expenses in connection with petroleum or natural gas.
The request of the company was that an allowance in respect of exploration development and preproduction expenses should be made. This could be done by the extension of section 83A to apply to surveying, exploration, development and preproduction activity pertaining to the creation and opening up of a new peat moss deposit.
Second, the company suggested a three year deferment of taxes on income for a new operation, and this could be done by amending section 83(5) and section 83(6). In the definitions in the subsection 6(a) of section 83, peat moss is not excluded. Those items which are excluded, except oil and gas wells which are dealt with elsewhere in the act, are not comparable to a peat moss operation. As was mentioned by the company's brief, peat bog development is a long and risky proposition. I know of some companies who have had to operate for three, four or even five years before they were in a position to export or to ship their products. In addition, the preproduction expenses of exploration, testing, surveying, drainage and bog development must be followed by a very sizeable capital investment in bog machinery, and in the last two or three years new machinery has been installed in existing peat moss industries at a very high price.
Third, this brief suggested the inclusion of assets used in production, such as are mentioned in class 10 of Schedule B of the Income Tax Act. In some instances, some of the peat moss operators have been claiming allowances, and in some cases the department has allowed such claims under class 10 of schedule B; but presently there is nothing in the act specifically permitting such companies to apply for a claim as suggested. With the considerable expansion and investment which is now taking place within the industry, we feel that it is most important and urgent to have such capital cost allowances specifically spelled out. As I mentioned earlier I know that in the last 24 months at least three operators in my constituency have installed machinery at considerable cost.

Ways and Means
Fourth, the brief suggests that a separate allowance be given under section 11(1) (b). This is the section that is referred to as the depletion allowance section, and it is based on net income attributable to mineral production. Peat moss is definitely a wasting or depleting asset. Once the peat is removed from a bog, it may take hundreds of years to replace it. Once a peat moss deposit is exhausted, all costs for development, plant, machinery, roadways and equipment must be written off as practically worthless, as is the case in any mining industry. So, Mr. Chairman, there is definitely a similarity between the exploration of peat moss and any mining operation.
As a last request the company suggested that shareholders of a corporation engaged in mining are allowed a deduction from dividends under section 11(2), and they therefore submitted that a similar deduction should be allowed to shareholders of a corporation engaged in the production of peat moss. Now, to support their contention that this should be considered as a mining classification, this company submitted a full and well detailed brief. I am not going to refer to this brief at this time, Mr. Chairman, but I should like to place on record the importance of this industry. Last year, for example, the total output of peat moss in Canada was 4 million bales, and a large percentage of this production was exported to the U.S. market. We notice that British Columbia produced 1,600,000 bales in this total production, Manitoba 550,000 bales, Ontario 200,000 bales, Quebec 800,000 bales, New Brunswick 750,000 bales, and Nova Scotia 100,000 bales. Therefore, it is a very important industry which deserves consideration, and I would ask the minister that special consideration be given to this request in order that this industry can continue to expand and provide additional labour, as it has done in the last few years.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman will have no difficulty in convincing anybody who is as proud of his Irish descent as I am of the importance of the industry to which he has referred. I know that some administrative action has been taken, the precise details of which I do not have immediately before me. However, I will draw to the attention of my colleague, the Minister of Finance, the representations which the hon. gentleman from Gloucester has made, and I can assure him that they will have the serious consideration of the Minister of Finance.
I wonder if we now might call these paragraphs individually. I am sure we will get on with our discussion more easily if we do so, and I am advised that that has been the usual practice.
[Mr. Robichaud.l

speechtext: If the committee is ready we will proceed to paragraph 1 of the Income Tax Act resolution.
Agreed.
I should like to speak briefly to the generality of the resolutions more particularly wtih respect to the research projects, oil and gas, preproduction expenses, and the logging tax.

With respect, I wonder if my hon. friend would permit us to come to those particular resolutions. I am advised than it has been the practice to call the individual paragraphs, and I will be glad to deal with each of the paragraphs as we go along. For example, scientific research is paragraph 3. The logging tax is in paragraph 5. I am sure we should make very much more satisfactory progress in that way. Otherwise I think we will open up a new and general debate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the committee
agreed that we would proceed to consider the income tax resolution on a paragraph by paragraph basis before the hon. member for Coast-Capilano rose to speak.

speechtext: I thought I had obtained it before the hon. member rose to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are on paragraph 1 now.
On paragraph 1-

Mr. Chairman, this paragraph provides for a $300 deduction in the case of a child who qualifies for family allowance, and $550 for other dependants. These dependants are children attending university, and they are dependant in other ways due to their inability to perform work of any description, or to make a living. Families with one or two children attending university, and who live in small towns such as those in my particular area, must send them many miles, up to 700 miles by rail or air, in order to attend university, and there are other expenses attached to their attendance such as living away from home, paying board, and so on. While appreciating the increase which has been allowed in this respect, I respectfully submit that further consideration should be given to this matter.
Then also there arises a new problem with respect to dependants or children who, because of one circumstance or another, are obliged to go into the United States in order to attend a university or a college. Either because of poor management on the part of

the present government or because of one reason or another our dollar has been devalued to a point where the cost is increased anywhere from $100 to $150 when the parent of this dependant is obliged to pay out $1,000 or $1,500 to United States institutions. That is the result of this serious depreciation in the value of the Canadian dollar.
This may sound unusual but I can assure the minister that before coming to the house in September I had made to me several representations asking if the government could not give some consideration for income tax purposes based on this unsatisfactory situation in which they were obliged to pay out something like $150 in excess of what they had been obliged to pay out in other years when the Canadian dollar was at par with the United States dollar.
I have said that we appreciate what is being done. I think the government is moving in the right direction with respect to income tax. I believe all income taxes are retrogressive. I hope that this will be a trend which we shall be able to set and that we shall be able to go even further when we sit on the opposite benches.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I hope any changes in the income tax law will not be so long delayed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall paragraph 1 carry?

Before it carries, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say one word if 1 may do so, and it is this. I of course agree completely with what the hon. member for Kootenay East has said about these very desirable deductions. However, there is one thing that I would point out, namely that these are deductions for taxpayers and that that the people who have the greatest need of all are those families whose incomes are below the taxpaying level and whose family allowances are being left unchanged while the allowances given to the taxpayers are being increased. Particularly with respect to families where children over 16 years of age are attending educational institutions, it seems to me that if the treasury can afford to do this, as they have indicated they can, then surely they can afford to do something for a group which cannot be very large, namely the children of families that are not even taxpayers themselves. In such cases that exist the family allowance should be extended during the whole period up to the age of 21 where they are attending educational institutions.

We appreciate what has been proposed in this first section relative to the
Ways and Means
increase in the amount deductible with respect to children. I still do not feel that this is a realistic figure in view of the increases in the cost of living and in everything that has to do with the education of our children. As I say, I do not think it is a realistic figure. I believe it ought to be increased.
Then as to the matter that has been raised with respect to the extension of the family allowance to include those who are continuing education, may I say I believe this is a worthwhile proposal. It is one that we have advanced for a considerable length of time. When a child is securing his higher education we feel that is about the time it is going to cost the most. For that reason we would very strongly urge that consideration be given to the extension of the family allowance to those who are continuing their education. As far as this figure is concerned, however, we believe that it should be revised upward because of the costs involved in preparing our young people to face the future.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I should like to add a few words but I do not know the rules of the house, and I understand that if the first part is passed today, it will not be possible to discuss it again later. I do not know if my information is correct.
However, as far as the tax deductions are concerned, I think the government does not go far enough.
If we consider tax exemptions in the case of children attending university and, as an hon. member mentioned earlier today some of those young people have to attend institutions of learning which are 700 or 800 miles away from their town or village-personally, I have one 3,500 miles from home-I maintain that the $550 deduction is not enough, particularly when compared to that of $300 granted for each child not attending university. Even that is not enough, because, at this time, the head of a family cannot live decently on the salary he earns, even if he were totally exempted from taxes.
And that is why we suggested exemptions of $3,000 for unmarried and $5,000 for married people. I think this is a progressive measure which will continue to progress, because as time passes, the exemptions become larger.
I think the members of this government might do a better job for the Canadian people. I would think that few people have sons or daughters attending university who cost them less than $1,500 to $2,000 a year.

Ways and Means
It is inconceivable that the government grants an exemption of only $550 a year for children who are studying, because, in such cases it is not always the rich who are giving their children an education.
Therefore, I repeat that the government is not generous enough with regard to exemptions granted for children attending university, in comparison to those who are not.
I think the government should revise that part of the Income Tax Act, so as to grant higher exemptions in the case I just mentioned, before allowing the total exemption.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I see the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. May I say to him that I am sorry that I did not see him previously.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for recognizing me. I have a number of remarks I wish to make by way of general discussion of the income tax resolution in particular. speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Shall paragraph 1 carry?
Paragraphs 1 and 2 agreed to.
On paragraph 3-

I think there is embodied here one of the more important resolutions consequent upon the budget. We are living in a day of technology. Indeed, I think most observant people would say that one of the chief problems confronting governments at every level is to see to it that technology and humanism can be compatible. Some of the more thoughtful people nowadays think we are having some difficulty in making them compatible. We are living in a world of tremendously rapid change. Although today we are not dealing with the humanism aspect, I would hope the government will not lose sight of it. We are dealing here with technology, its promises, its threats and its benefits to mankind. Unfortunately we must constantly relate this item to the budget which is not a budget, upon which we are working in relation to all budgetary matters. I come back to the budget that was presented to us, that is, the revised estimates, and I want to relate this resolution to the work of the national research council. Here we have a
situation where the government is making this provision, and I should like to put it on the
record again:
That with respect to its first taxation year ending after April 10, 1962 and the next succeeding four taxation years a corporation be permitted to deduct in computing income 150 per cent of the amount by which expenditures of a current and capital nature on scientific research in Canada incurred by it in the year exceed expenditures of a current and capital nature on scientific research in Canada incurred by it in its last taxation year ending on or before April 10, 1962.
This is one of those decisions that has been made by a government constantly confronted with the necessity of using sticks and carrots as an inducement. This is a carrot procedure. This is encouragement to industries in Canada to spend a great deal more on research than they are spending at the present time and to that extent it is a very laudable procedure and will receive the support of those on this side of the house. At the same time we are not going to lose the opportunity to point out that it is a pitifully small amount of money and a pitifully inadequate attempt that is being made at this time to restore research at the various levels in Canada to levels commensurate with what is being done for research in other countries that are advancing rapidly.
So I refer to the revised estimates in respect of the national research council and I find that there is an increase totalling $2,030,000 of which all but $1 million is by way of increases in salaries. I think I can read into this a belated appreciation on the part of the government that they simply had to increase salaries in the national research council most appreciably if they were going to retain the services of the splendid men they have there at the present time. There is an increase of $1 million in the revised estimates which is called assistance toward research in industry.
The resolution that we are dealing with here provides, and I think adequately, for some recompense for those industries in Canada that at present have research facilities and it will encourage them to increase their research. It may have the effect of bringing back from the United States some of those thousands of splendid Canadians who have gone there to work in research and who are working for parent companies of companies operating in Canada. It may even have that effect, and to that extent I say it is most commendable.
But let us go beyond these powerful Canadian companies which have the ability to pay the cost of research and would probably add additional amounts to their research budgets regardless of whether or not this resolution became law. What are we doing for the
[Mr. Ouellet.l

innumerable small companies which are just as dependant upon research today as the large companies are and probably more so, many of whom have no ability whatsoever to set up their own research departments and whose principals must occupy their time fully keeping store instead of going into research?
Surely it is obvious that this provision of $1 million in the national research council estimates is for their benefit, $1 million for all of Canada presumably to assist the small businessman, the small manufacturer, in devising ways and means of making his business more efficient and more profitable. For that purpose we are setting aside the generous sum, in the view of the government, of $1 million.
Is that not something to start with?

Yes, it is something, but let me tell the hon. member that it is a very small pebble in the pond. Let me tell hon. members that on defence research alone the United States is expending $6 billion this year. Eleven per cent of their stupendous defence budget goes for research alone. I am fairly closely in touch with one of the universities of the United States, one which has become a little more notorious than famous, the University of Mississippi. I can tell hon. members that $8 million was thrown at that university this year and they were told to spend it. Tremendous sums of money have flowed from the defence budget of the United States to all their universities and they have been told to spend the money. They are spending it, and I am sure that the minister and the parliamentary assistant are aware that these universities have teams now throughout Canada trying to pick up the best Canadian brains to go to the United States.
I want to remind hon. members of what has gone on in that regard because a tremendous number of Canadians have gone to the United States in very recent years. As a matter of fact the Labour Gazette of January 31, 1962 makes the statement that in the period from 1950 to 1960 a total of 42,000 professional and technical workers emigrated from Canada to the United States. A more recent story in the Financial Post, a copy of which I could not obtain, pointed out that 5,600 of the most highly educated Canadians, including some 650 doctors, I believe, went to the United States in the past year.

Mr. Speaker, as I said, I should like to be very brief in order to facilitate as much as possible the second reading of this bill.
I know that several members had indicated their desire to take the floor, in order to favour in some way Bill No. C-17 which is now before us. So, for my part, I have decided to be very brief in order not to give the impression that we wish to talk it out. That is why I have suggested to my good friends who definitely want to help civil servants, so that they maybe considered as first class individuals in this country, that their silence might be much more eloquent than their speeches, since we want this bill to be voted upon as soon as possible.
However, if it is to be talked out, if we must discuss it until six o'clock, well, I would like the odious responsibility to fall upon the shoulders of those who are not in favour of the civil servants to talk it out.
Mr. Speaker, the bill in question was introduced as an amendment last year, when we passed the new Civil Service Act.
It had then been proposed that section 7, as it now stands, should be amended, since it was not favourable to civil servants, because it says:
(1) The Minister of Finance or such members of the public service as he may designate shall from time to time consult with representatives of appropriate organizations and associations of employees.
This means that only the minister or those whom he may designate are entitled to engage in discussions, but that the employees shall never have the right to invite the government to discuss with them. This is like a one way street from which you cannot back out, once you are there.
I recall having pointed out last year that I did not approve of this attitude, but civil servants were willing to accept it, try it out and see whether or not it worked. It was tried out and has proved a failure, because not very long ago, when employees asked for an interview with the former minister of

finance (Mr. Fleming) who is now Minister of Justice, in order to discuss an increase for the 55,000 employees who had received none, there were meetings and discussions. I remember that, a certain Monday night, reporters asked civil service employees: "Is there anything new?", and they were answered: "No, because we have to meet again tomorrow morning".
Now, on Tuesday morning, before the meeting, the Minister of Finance announced that, because of that policy-how do you call it, I know it is going to hurt some people when it is called an austerity program-well, because of the austerity program, they would not receive the increase. Then, the spokesmen of the civil service associations had to go home, as the minister refused to pursue discussions.
The bill I submit at this time demands that civil service employees, like the government, be authorized to have discussions and further stipulates that if they do not succeed in agreeing on the various clauses, they resort to arbitration.
I did not mention details with regard to arbitration, so as to keep the bill as simple as possible. We always might resort to a recognized arbitration system: a representative appointed by the government, a representative appointed by the associations and a third person appointed by both, which would represent the government and the associations to the satisfaction of both parties or by the governor in council if they were unable to come to an agreement. Anyway, people want them to have recourse to arbitration.
The following argument was brought up in several circles: "The crown cannot be forced to accept an order from any other body other than parliament".
Well, Mr. Speaker, I must say that England has not been so touchy, because it has accepted this measure. It has granted the right to arbitration to its employees. Australia has done the same, as well as New Zealand. Is Canada more touchy, with regards to the crown than England, New Zealand and Australia? I do not think so. Besides, I have been careful to put in the bill a provision for the protection of the government which must take the final decision. I have been careful to provide that if an agreement was not reached, if the negotiations did not result in agreement, the matter under dispute would be taken to an arbitration tribunal and that the arbitration decision would be subject, if necessary, to the approval of parliament regarding the rates of pay for each grade and the establishment of

the allowances. In this way, parliament will have the last say. Parliament will decide, without appeal, if we must accept or reject the sentence of the arbitration tribunal.
I remember that last year, when we brought forward the amendments, the official spokesman of the government was the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell). This is what he had to say:
But this is not necessary, since we already have consultation possibilities in section 7.
Well, as I have said, this has not been successful and the employees have not received satisfaction.
Today, the employees are insisting. They are entitled to arbitration, which is a natural right above the laws. People have the right to protect their interests.
Civil servants are not asking for the right to go on strike, which is implied in the act. For, according to an English principle, that which is not excluded is included. However, except for post office employees, and they did not insist, civil servants have not asked for this right.
The others here did not ask for it: the brief of the Civil Service Federation of Canada and the other, submitted by the Canadian postal employees, did not exactly ask for the right to strike. But what they wanted was the right to complain, when they felt wronged and to be able to turn to a body empowered to consider their grievances independently and to make a recommendation to the parliament of this country whose decision would be final.
One province has now set up a body responsible for negotiations and recognizes the right to strike. I am thinking of Saskatchewan.
As far as negotiation and arbitration are concerned, the system does not exist in any province; it is under consideration in British Columbia and I think they will have it before long.
As to consultation between employees and the government within joint councils, it exists in New Brunswick and Ontario as well as in Manitoba and Alberta.
The provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Ontario and British Columbia allow consultations between employees' organizations and the civil service commission.
The provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Quebec authorize direct representation to the government by employees' organizations.
I believe this is the first time a parliament has ever had the opportunity to give civil servants the right to be considered as

Civil Service Act
first class citizens, and have the right to turn them down. I do not feel that we could turn down members of all other organizations.
That is why I ask hon. members to be short in their praise of the civil service so that this bill might be passed.
If someone or some political party should be held responsible for depriving them of that right, I want it to be understood that it is the party that will assume such responsibility and not those who really want the civil servants to be considered as first class citizens.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill of the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron) is very appropriate since it is intended to grant civil servants the same privilege as enjoyed by employees of non-government corporations, that is the right to collective bargaining and to arbitration in case of disagreement. In principle, nothing in this bill is contrary to the good operation of government business.
Personally, I am of the opinion that every employee should be able, directly or through union representatives, to discuss working conditions with his boss and secure by contract the respect of arrangements agreed to by both parties.
To a certain extent, what has been found beneficial to free enterprise employees should also apply to civil servants. I say to a certain extent, because there is a difference between the requirements of free enterprise and those of the government. While an employee in industry or business must earn some profit for his employer, the public servant must first of all produce quality which cannot be measured by instruments, let alone by statistics. Although parliament is indeed the actual employer, the public servant is at the same time his own boss because he has to pay taxes just like the employee in free enterprise.
Parliament is made up of politicians-honest politicians, let us say for the purpose of this discussion-who, to fulfil their mandate properly, must constantly call upon public servants. Dependant as members of the house are upon those public servants, it becomes impossible for parliament to be completely objective when this house has to deal with the problems of the civil servants. They can only be judged by public opinion.
Consequently, this harsh, pitiless and often cruel judge-public opinion-is the best
[Mr. Caron.)
guardian of the efficiency and honesty which must exist in the public administration and is a contributing factor in keeping politicians on the straight and narrow path.
To date in Canada, public opinion always favoured civil servants. Except during the war years, when our friends opposite set up controls and multiplied jobs in all government agencies, the civil service of Canada always maintained its good reputation.
To give an opportunity to all civil servants to negotiate working agreements with the governor in council today would be a way of appreciating the good and loyal services of the great majority of those people who spend their lives serving the nation.
There should, however, be a reservation and that is the right to strike, as the hon. member for Hull was saying a while ago. If in industry the right to strike is the only efficient way for the unions to obtain something from a stubborn employer, the security of employment enjoyed by civil servants should make up for the recourse to reprisals. As an employer the government does not have to meet the same competition as private enterprise, and its employees in turn do not have the same worries as workers in industry who can lose their jobs at any moment or may have to change trades because of some development in some section of industry or because of radical technical changes.
The right to strike is a necessary evil of labour unions to fight the selfishness and greed of some employers; on the other hand, the government as an employer is above profit seeking and the general welfare of all citizens is at stake, so the right to strike is not justified in the civil service.
I wish to point out, Mr. Speaker, a fact that shows the great progress about to take place with regard to the salaries of the civil servants: that is proved by a plank in the platform announced by Mr. Johnson, the next premier of Quebec. It will enable the provincial civil servants in Quebec to negotiate and enter into collective bargaining with the government. That is an initiative that will go down in history and which, once again, will have come from the Union Nationale party.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Hull is not proposing this bill solely to win the friendship of the many civil servants who live in his riding-

This bill has to do with the welfare of a large number of Canadian citizens employed in the public service of this country. I believe developments and events of recent times have emphasized the necessity for making changes in the procedure whereby good and amicable relations can be maintained between the government and its employees and more adequate provision made for the dispensation of justice as far as grievances are concerned.

These people are all very concerned about the position in which they find themselves in their relationship with the government.

Reference has been made to the wage freeze which was clamped on by the government because of its austerity program. In spite of the fact that certain recommendations had been made, and that these people had more or less received assurances that consideration would be given to their requests, they found, instead, that those requests had been turned down, and this has resulted in a great deal of discontent and hardship.
I believe these various grievances which are felt by civil servants, as they are by workers in other fields, are very pressing. Therefore I wish to express myself as being in agreement with the principle of this bill which is to the effect that facilities should be provided whereby civil servants would have more attention paid to their problems and to their needs. I should only like to add that some of these associations which have written to me recognize that there are certain areas in which the rights accorded to workers in other fields may not be applicable to civil servants. They have indicated, in this regard, that they were not pressing for the right to strike. At least one of the communications makes this proviso. Industry in this country has for years accepted the principle of negotiation, and in fact has been encouraged and urged to do so by various levels of government in this country. Therefore, I see no reason why members of the civil service should not also enjoy this privilege of being able to negotiate with the government.
It also seems to me that in the case of the civil service where, to my mind at least, the idea of a strike is unthinkable, arbitration would be the logical step in the event of a breakdown in negotiation. However, there is one point about this bill. I am not entirely sure of the technical aspects of the bill, but subsection (3) of the proposed section 7 says:
The results of such negotiation and/or arbitration shall be proclaimed by a suitable instrument, where necessary subject to the approval of parliament.
I am not sure I understand the significance of that, but it seems to me that if you

accept the principle of arbitration, then the decision reached by arbitration must be final, and I question whether it should even be referred back again to parliament. I say that because if a civil service body takes a question right through to arbitration, surely that should be the final point and the parties can count on having a decision made which will be binding. I think I would have preferred, and I say this with all due respect to the hon. member who has introduced this bill, to have had him move a resolution rather than a bill at this time, because if the resolution were passed it would have allowed the government to write its own legislation in this matter. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, now that the hon. member who presented the bill has flushed a couple of members who have expressed their opposition to it perhaps I might say a word in support of it. The question raised by the bill is simply whether employees of the government of Canada are going to have the right to bargain collectively. This bill will give them that right, a right which they do not now enjoy, and for that reason members of this party support it. It is for the same reason that the hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), when he was premier of Saskatchewan, gave the employees of that province the right to bargain collectively.
The right to bargain collectively is a fundamental human right that ought to be enjoyed by people who work for a living whether they work for private industry, or for the government of Canada or that of any province. It is simply a question whether or not they are going to be second class citizens. We think they should no longer have to suffer that status. We want to make them first class citizens, and that is why we support the bill.
I would draw the attention of the hon. member for Hull who introduced the bill to the fact that it does not provide any 27507-3-80J
Civil Service Act
machinery of arbitration, which I suggest to him is absolutely essential. This bill simply expresses a principle. We agree with that principle and that is why we support the bill. We respectfully point out, however, that it does have that deficiency.
The present consultative procedure does not really bring into being any kind of genuine collective bargaining situation. It is bound to be simply an artificial kind of bargaining so long as the salaries, wages and working conditions of civil servants are determined in the last analysis by the people occupying the treasury benches. There is a certain artificiality about negotiations carried on in that kind of atmosphere. The prospect of arbitration binding upon the government of Canada as well as upon civil servants is the greatest inducement to both sides to conduct genuine negotiations, and the creation of machinery to provide arbitration would induce both sides to carry on bona fide collective bargaining.
I was interested to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley support this proposal because in my own province, from which he also comes, a report dealing with the status of civil servants in that province was submitted to the government approximately three years ago by a distinguished professor of law at the University of British Columbia. The report, it is widely suspected, recommended that collective bargaining rights should be given to civil servants in that province; but Premier Bennett, in his usual frank and open way, has kept the report hidden for three years.
The thing that is important in my opinion is to prevent wages and salaries of civil servants becoming a political issue. Because the government has not provided arbitration the present wage freeze has become a political issue. The only way to prevent that is to provide for binding arbitration, and that is why we support the bill. I urge members on the government side to let the question be called when I have finished my remarks, as I have done.

-I want to say in one minute that I also agree with the principle of the bill and I congratulate the hon. member for Hull upon introducing it. In the few seconds I have left I wish to say that I think the government has an obligation to bring in legislation based to a large degree on this principle. As we have heard, there are many suggestions as to how we might improve
it. We might want to have a further look at the system in Great Britain.
I also suggest that the question of arbitration is another area that requires examination; but in supporting the principle of the bill I wish to impress on those members of my own party who occupy the front benches that I think they have a responsibility to extend the same freedom to civil servants as has been extended throughout the rest of Canada by industry. I respectfully ask the hon. members who sit on the front benches to take note that there is one member on the back benches who considers this is something that should be done.

subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL APPOINTING ROYAL COMMISSION ON PILOTAGE

speechtext:
Certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting of the committee of the privy council, approved by His Excellency the Governor General on the 1st November 1962.
The committee of the privy council, on the recommendation of the Right Honourable John George Diefenbaker, the Prime Minister, advise that:
The Honourable Yves Bernier, a judge of the superior court of Quebec, Quebec, P.Q.
Robert Knowlton Smith, Esq., Waterloo, Ontario
Harold Alexander Renwick, Esq., Vancouver, British Columbia
be appointed commissioners under part I of the Inquiries Act, to inquire into and report upon the problems relating to marine pilotage provided in Canada, more particularly under the Canada Shipping Act, and to recommend the changes, if any, that should be made in the pilotage system now prevailing, having regard to safety of navigation, development of shipping and commerce, the interests of pilots, shipowners, masters and the public generally; and in particular, without restricting the generality of the foregoing, the commission shall consider and report upon:
(a)	the extent and nature of marine pilotage requirements, including compulsory pilotage, compulsory payment of pilotage dues and the granting of exemptions;
(b)	the duties, responsibilities and status of marine pilots; and
(c)	the adequacy of the organizational structure provided in the Canada Shipping Act for
the administration, regulations and financing of pilotage, taking into consideration such factors as the provision of pilotage services, the determination, collection and disposal of pilotage dues, and the entry into service, technical standards, conduct, income, welfare and pension arrangements of pilots.
The committee further advise:
1.	That the commissioners be authorized to exercise all the powers conferred upon them by section 11 of the Inquiries Act and be assisted to the fullest extent by government departments and agencies;
2.	That the commissioners adopt such procedures and methods as they may from time to time deem expedient for the proper conduct of the inquiry and sit at such times and at such places in Canada as they may decide from time to time;
3.	That the commissioners be authorized to engage the services of such counsel, staff and technical advisers as they may require at rates of remuneration and reimbursement to be approved by the treasury board;
4.	That the commissioners report to the governor in council with all reasonable dispatch, and file with the dominion archivist the papers and records of the commission as soon as reasonably may be after the conclusion of the inquiry; and
5.	That the Honourable Mr. Justice Bernier be chairman of the commission.
R. B. Bryce,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
Monday, November 5, 1962
